How this book works

Routes through the book, the running example, and the rules for reading source claims.

625 words in this guideFour source labelsIndependent study

This is a source study, not product documentation. It explains why DeepSeek Harness is built the way it is, moving from the problem each mechanism solves to the code that implements it. The source is frozen at one commit so the line references stay meaningful.

Three reading paths

The full path. Read in order. Each part adds one layer to the failing-test request.

The builder's path. Read chapters 3 through 6, then 7 and 8. Together they cover the loop, the log, context, tools, trust, and durability. Use chapter 2 when you need to understand how those parts get mounted.

The architecture path. Read chapter 1, chapter 2, chapter 11, and the diagrams in chapters 3, 4, and 10. It gives the shape and the trade-offs without the full implementation detail.

The running example

A developer asks the agent to fix a failing discount test in src/cart.ts and run the cart tests. The example is invented. It keeps the mechanics concrete across chapters without pretending to be a recorded session.

The same request becomes:

  • one turn with several steps;
  • a sequence of tool calls and durable results;
  • a growing session log with a surface projection;
  • a prompt assembled from sections, tools, and runtime facts;
  • two permission decisions and one sandbox policy;
  • a durable record that can survive a crash;
  • a job that could be delegated to a child agent;
  • a live conversation in the browser.

Source labels

The book uses four labels when the distinction matters.

  • Source marks an exact quotation from the pinned commit.
  • Walkthrough marks an explanation of a path inferred from code. The path is real; the prose around it is the author's.
  • Teaching model marks a simplification made to expose a mechanism.
  • Assumption marks values, timings, or UI states invented for an interaction.

Inline source references look like packages/core/agent-loop/src/agent.ts:298-397. Every one links to the exact file and line range at commit 687f282. Source tables at the end of each chapter list the main references.

What is not claimed

DeepSeek Harness is in developer preview. The book describes version 0.2.1-rc.2 at one commit. Later versions may rename types, reorder the loop, or change an interface. The source is the authority.

The book is independent. It is not affiliated with DeepSeek, and it is not a security review. Plugin compatibility checks are not a sandbox, and the approval and sandbox chapters say where those boundaries end.

No test result appears in the prose unless the result came from a command that was actually run. Test files are cited as evidence of intended coverage, not as proof that a behavior passed.

Source snapshot. Project commit 687f282e8625c6b8d11ff58211a90524be2e4317 (2026-10-17, version 0.2.1-rc.2). Research date: 2026-10-21. A note on depth

Each chapter has a main line that can be read without stopping, followed by source mapping and trade-offs. Fenced source excerpts are short. Most implementation detail stays in prose and diagrams so the reader can keep the mechanism in view.

The goal is predictive understanding. You should finish able to see how a new behavior would fit, where it would fail, and which existing boundary it would cross. The book does not attempt complete package coverage.

Part I · The Shape/Chapter 01

A Harness Made of Replaceable Parts

Why an agent runtime becomes a plugin tree, a log, and a set of seams.

≈ 11 min read3 figures1 interactionSource 687f282e
In this chapter · 10 sections
  1. The job
  2. Two shapes
  3. Three bets
  4. The system on one page
  5. The failing test, end to end
  6. What the loop does not own
  7. Costs and limits
  8. How to read this book
  9. Source map
  10. What carries forward

A language model can describe a file edit. It cannot open the file. It can propose a shell command. It cannot spawn the process. It has no durable memory of the last session unless something gives it one. The software that closes that gap is the harness: the process that assembles context, calls the model, executes tools, records what happened, asks for human decisions, and presents the result.

DeepSeek Harness (dsh) is an open-source harness for coding agents. It is built on an unusual premise. The model adapter, tool registry, session log, policy layer, Web server, and agent loop are all plugins composed at boot. The repository calls this architecture "everything is a plugin." That phrase is accurate, but it hides the useful question: what does the plugin boundary buy, and what does it cost?

This chapter builds the answer from the job a harness has to do. It then maps the parts of DeepSeek Harness and follows one request through all of them. The rest of the book zooms into those parts in the order a request meets them.

The job

Consider what a coding agent needs in order to complete this request:

The discount test is failing after the tax change. Find the cause, fix src/cart.ts, and run the cart tests.

The agent must:

  • turn the request into a model call with the right instructions, history, and tool schemas;
  • stream the response while keeping partial output visible;
  • detect requested tool calls and execute reads, edits, and a test command;
  • send the tool results back to the model and repeat until the model stops asking;
  • keep a record complete enough to resume, audit, and display later;
  • ask a human before actions the deployment does not trust;
  • contain the blast radius of commands on the local machine;
  • report progress to a terminal or browser without becoming the source of truth;
  • survive cancellation, provider errors, malformed tool input, and process death.

The smallest useful implementation is a loop around a model, a map of tools, and a message array. That design works in a demo. Pressure arrives quickly. A second model provider needs a different stream vocabulary. A remote sandbox needs a different filesystem and subprocess implementation. A team wants per-session tool restrictions. A browser client needs to replay an in-progress turn. A crash must preserve the edit that already happened.

Each requirement changes a different part of the process. In a monolith, each change also reaches into the loop.

Two shapes

The first design choice is where variation lives.

In a fixed application, the loop imports the model client and the tool implementations. Configuration selects behavior inside code the application already owns. New behavior means editing the application.

In a plugin composition, the process starts with an empty list of entries. Layers add plugin rows. A row names a module and its configuration. Plugins register services and behavior on a shared context. Other plugins declare which services they require. Activation follows dependencies, not a hand-written startup order.

The composition shape moves cost to the boundaries. You need a lifecycle for plugins, a way to discover services, a policy for failed activation, and rules for reversing registrations. You gain the ability to replace the provider, the toolset, or the whole surface without forking the loop.

DeepSeek Harness uses Cordis, a small TypeScript plugin framework, for those boundaries. Five ideas are enough for this book. A plugin is an object with an apply function or a Service subclass. A context is a repository of services addressed by stable keys such as ctx.tools and ctx.sessions. A plugin declares dependencies through inject, so it waits until those services exist. Plugins communicate through typed events, including waterfalls where listeners wrap the next handler and can allow, deny, or replace a result. Registrations are effects: removing the plugin or disposing the context undoes what it added.

docs/cordis-primer.md:7-16

docs/cordis-primer.md:29-35

The effect lifecycle also changes boot. A plugin can be loaded, wait for a missing service, activate later, and unload in a defined order. A plugin can be loaded, wait for a missing service, activate later, and unload in a defined order. A failed plugin has a fiber with a recorded error. A registration made through the agent's scoped context disappears when that agent is torn down. The same machinery supports configuration reloads and per-agent capability sets.

Three bets

The source describes a running dsh as "a plugin tree composed at boot from ordered layers."docs/architecture.md:13-25 That sentence contains the architecture's first bet. The product is a composition recipe, not one executable tree. The web, headless, sdk, and acp products are predefined profiles over a shared base. sdk-minimal is the deliberate exception: one bundle owns its complete tree and does not apply dsh-base. A profile is stored in the Harness home; a bundle distributes a patch layer. Later layers can replace a row's configuration by id. Boot applies the layers to an empty root, then lets the loader activate whatever can find its dependencies.

The second bet concerns truth. The session log is append-only, and model history is a projection of it. Model-visible means logged: any fact the model sees must be reconstructable from a durable session event. The log also carries non-message facts such as request/header, tool calls, and turn boundaries. The browser transcript, resume, fork, and audit views derive from the same record, each through its own projection.

The third bet concerns capability boundaries. A seam has a service definition, a provider, and a consumer.docs/architecture.md:130-136 Filesystem, subprocess, sandbox, approval, model streaming, persistence, and subagents all have seams. Policy is often a consumer of a seam rather than a special case inside the loop. A provider swap can move Bash, PTY, and language-server work into a remote execution world without rewriting the tools.

The bets reinforce one another. A plugin tree needs stable service contracts to be replaceable. A durable log gives those contracts a shared factual base. Seams keep the loop from importing every implementation. None of the bets is free. The plugin tree adds indirection and lifecycle complexity. The log adds storage and projection work. Seams add interface design and versioning. The book returns to those costs in every chapter.

The system on one page

Read the map from left to right.

Composition is the boot layer. Profiles, bundles, and patches decide which plugins exist. app-boot composes the rows and starts the loader. The loader owns activation, waiting, and failure reporting.

The loop is the narrow spine. dsh-agent publishes the Agent contract and the live registry. dsh-agent-loop registers the concrete driver on that seam when mounted. The driver owns the inbox, turn and step progression, model attempts, and tool scheduling.

State is the session record. dsh-session stores typed events in memory and derives model messages from the surface projection. dsh-session-persistence and its JSONL provider make the record durable. Prompt assembly (dsh-system-prompt) and the tool registry (dsh-tools) supply the request envelope.

Capabilities are the seams through which the agent acts. A model adapter streams tokens and tool calls. The tool registry executes them. Approval decides whether a call may proceed. Sandboxing wraps subprocess arguments. Filesystem and subprocess providers can run locally or remotely.

The surface is not the source of truth. The Web client follows the durable session journal, maintains its own models, and renders registered views. The CLI and browser receive different projections of the same events.

The separation is visible in the package keys. No core loop package imports the Web client, the JSONL session format, or the local sandbox. Those are rows in a composition.

The failing test, end to end

The first request in the scenario arrives through agent.followup(). That method does not call the model. It writes an inbox splice into the session and wakes the driver.packages/core/agent-loop/src/agent.ts:154-180 This distinction matters later: pending input is durable state, and waking is a scheduling decision.

  1. The driver opens a turn with turn/start.
  2. At the turn boundary it claims all pending next-step input and one queued follow-up. In this case, the follow-up is the user's request.
  3. It assembles prompt sections and tools, then runs the agent/pre-step waterfall. A listener may reject the step or rewrite the input.
  4. step/start opens the step. The loop resolves the model route, admits the rendered system prompt and user messages to the log, records a request/header, derives history from the log, and freezes the request.
  5. The adapter streams the assistant response. The loop publishes live chunks through agent/assistant-stream, but it records the settled message as assistant/message with the compact timed stream.
  6. The model asks to read the test and source files. The loop appends each tool/call before execution. The tool registry runs policy, dispatch, and post-processing; the loop appends a tool/result for each call.
  7. The two results create another model request. The loop reaches four model steps: reads, edit, test, and a final answer. Three tool batches are recorded, and the turn stays open while tools keep producing another request.
  8. When the model stops emitting tool calls, the step ends. agent/turn-stopping gets one last chance to extend or stop the turn. The driver writes turn/end.
  9. Persistence flushes at its next checkpoint. The browser has already rendered live chunks and durable events; on refresh it reconstructs the same conversation from the session journal.

Two properties are easy to miss. The turn, not the user message, is the unit of work. One prompt can produce many model calls. And the model request is built from the log at the boundary, not from a mutable conversation object held by the loop. Those choices make retries, resume, and replay possible, and they shape the next ten chapters.

What the loop does not own

The loop is the spine, but it is a thin one. It does not know which model vendor is behind the adapter. It does not know whether a tool's body runs locally or over SSH. It does not render a browser. It asks ctx.approval when a policy listener returns ask; it calls ctx.tools to execute a call; it uses ctx.sessions for the log.

That division keeps the critical path readable. It also means a reader cannot understand one behavior by reading one file. A denied tool call passes through the tool registry, an approval service, and perhaps a sandbox provider. A resumed turn passes through persistence, repair, session reconstruction, and the loop. The book follows those paths rather than presenting packages alphabetically.

Costs and limits

A composition architecture is not automatically more modular than a monolith. The boundaries only help when contracts stay narrow and lifecycle rules are enforced. DeepSeek Harness pays for its flexibility in several visible ways.

YAML is now an interface. A profile has a bundle order, patch precedence, and rows that can be replaced or inserted. The user can inspect the effective tree with dsh --profile web --dump-config, but a misordered patch still produces a valid-looking configuration with the wrong behavior.

Activation is asynchronous. A plugin can be loaded but waiting for a service, so "present in config" is not the same as "running." Startup has to distinguish optional failures from required ones. The loop's own startup depends on services that may arrive from several bundles.

The log is a second representation of every interaction. It must be validated, projected, frozen, and persisted. A message replacement has to preserve identities and ordering. A browser view has to distinguish model history from human transcript.

Seams move design effort into interfaces. A provider cannot be only "the local one"; it has to satisfy a contract that also works over a remote execution world. Some seams are intentionally narrow, and the narrowness shows up as limitations.

A plugin boundary is also not a security boundary. In-process plugins share the Node process and can access the same resources. Version compatibility checks reduce accidental breakage; they do not sandbox malicious package code. The approval and sandbox chapters treat security separately from modularity.

How to read this book

The chapters follow the path of the failing-test request:

  • Part I explains how the tree gets there. Chapter 2 composes a profile and boots it.
  • Part II follows the request. Chapter 3 covers turns and steps, chapter 4 the log, chapter 5 context assembly, and chapter 6 tool execution.
  • Part III covers the boundaries that make action defensible and durable. Chapter 7 covers approval and sandboxing; chapter 8 covers crashes and resume.
  • Part IV scales outward and upward. Chapter 9 delegates to child agents, chapter 10 follows the session into the browser, and chapter 11 extracts the transferable design choices.

A reader who wants the shape first can read this chapter, the three diagrams in chapter 3, and chapter 11. A reader who wants to build a smaller harness should read chapters 3 through 6 closely. A reader evaluating the architecture should watch for the cost sections: they are where the design stops being a slogan.

What carries forward

A harness becomes replaceable by separating three things that are easy to tangle: the flow of work, the record of what happened, and the capabilities used to act. DeepSeek Harness gives the flow a small driver, the record a typed append-only log, and the capabilities service contracts. The plugin tree is the mechanism that assembles the three without a privileged application object.

The next chapter starts before the first model call. A process that composes itself has to answer a boot question: which parts are present, and what happens when one of them is not.

Part I · The Shape/Chapter 02

The Program Is a Composition

Profiles, bundles, patches, activation, and the shape of startup failure.

≈ 11 min read3 figures1 interactionSource 687f282e
In this chapter · 8 sections
  1. A tree with no privileged root
  2. Booting the web profile
  3. Where the mechanism lives
  4. What fails, and who decides
  5. What is required, chosen, or inherited
  6. The cost of composability
  7. What carries forward
  8. Source map

A developer opens the storefront repository and runs dsh web. A browser tab appears. The process behind it can read src/cart.ts, run pnpm vitest, and append every step to a session log. The same installed command can run dsh --profile headless "run the tests" and print one answer, or serve an ACP client or an SDK client over stdio. The repository and its files are the book's running example, not a real run.

Producing four products from one command is not the hard part. The products share most parts and differ in a few: a browser transport, a one-shot runner, a JSON-RPC server, an ACP bridge. The hard part is composing them so the shared parts stay shared and the differing parts stay replaceable. Separate applications would copy the shared parts and wire every plugin four times. One application with flags would move the product boundary into code, where a user cannot replace a part. The CLI README states the contract: "SDK and ACP are profiles, not separate public bins."apps/cli/README.md:5

The composition must be inspectable before it runs, admit third-party plugins without patching a privileged core, resolve dependencies without a hand-maintained order, and classify failures: a missing optional provider and a missing agent loop are different events.

This chapter sits at the boot boundary. Nothing here calls a model or opens a session. It decides which plugins will be alive when the storefront request arrives.

A tree with no privileged root

DSH builds on Cordis. A plugin is a module with an apply(ctx) function or a Service subclass. A service is a capability registered under a stable key such as ctx.tools. A plugin declares inject, so it waits for those services. Registrations are effects with disposers; unloading reverses what a plugin added. A fiber is one plugin's activation state, from pending to disposed.docs/cordis-primer.md:9-13

A profile is a named composition under $DSH_HOME/profiles/<name>. It declares an ordered bundle list and holds the user's patch file. A bundle is an npm package declaring dsh.bundle.patch, one patch file or an ordered list. A patch is a YAML operation list: insert rows, or target a row by id and replace fields. A layer is one patch source in application order. An entry is one row the Loader mounts: id, module specifier, optional config, inject, and disabled. The Loader owns the entry tree and imports the modules.packages/boot/app-boot/src/profile.ts:36-40

The profile's root config is an empty YAML array. cordis.yml contains []. Every config row in the composed tree was inserted by a layer, and every layer above can target it by id. The exception is the bootstrap include entry that mounts the file; it is app glue, not a config row.packages/boot/app-boot/src/index.ts:769-783 There is no base configuration outside the patch order whose rows a user patch cannot reach. The empty root is a design choice, not a law of plugin systems. It follows from replaceability: a layer-inserted row has a source, a stable id, and a later layer that can override it.apps/cli/src/profile-boot.ts:80-85

A patch replaces fields rather than merging them. An insert appends rows to the root or a named group. A non-insert patch finds the row by id and assigns the keys it names. A config key replaces the whole config object. A patch that names no existing row warns and is skipped, and a later patch can target a row an earlier patch inserted. Whole-field replacement forces an override to restate every field it keeps.vendor/include/src/index.ts:76-124

The order is explicit:

Actual source, profile-context.ts:75-80

TypeScript
const patches = structuredClone([
  ...readBundlePatches(binName, context, initialProfile),
  ...(initialProfile?.patches ?? loadOptionalPatches(binName, context.patchPath) ?? []),
  ...(loadOptionalPatches(binName, join(context.home, PROFILE_PATCH_FILENAME)) ?? []),
  ...context.overlays,
])

Bundles first, in dsh.profile.bundles order; then the profile patch; then the home patch; then --patch overlays. The launcher can add a synthesized telemetry disable patch last. The web bundle declares five patch files, applied in the listed order: the host rows, then four agent-preset declarations.packages/bundle/web-app/package.json:46-56

Teaching model. The pseudocode below leaves out the package table, the version compatibility check, the telemetry patch, and activation. It shows only how row lists compose.

Text
composeRows(profile, home, argv):
  rows = []
  for bundle in profile.bundles:
    for file in bundle.patchFiles:
      rows = apply(rows, parse(file))
  rows = apply(rows, parse(profile.patch))
  rows = apply(rows, parse(home.patch))
  for overlay in argv:
    rows = apply(rows, parse(overlay))
  return rows

Booting the web profile

dsh web is shorthand: the parser rewrites a leading non-flag token into --profile web and leaves everything after the launcher's flags to the app. The launcher knows --profile, --patch, and the dump flags, not --port. That flag is parsed inside the tree by the web-startup plugin, which provides webStartup; the webserver and web-runtime rows inject it. Headless, SDK, and ACP follow the same pattern.apps/cli/src/args.ts:4-11

Booting web resolves $DSH_HOME/profiles/web. On first use, the directory is initialized from the shipped template with dsh-base and dsh-web-app.packages/boot/app-boot/src/profile.ts:179-195 Every boot loads the manifest, resolves each bundle from the installation first and the profile second, reads its patch files and the profile patch. A bundle that cannot be resolved, read, or admitted by the version check is skipped and listed in skippedBundles; the rest keep their order.packages/boot/app-boot/src/profile.ts:751-774 The launcher then rewrites cordis.yml to []. The file is an include anchor, not a row store; a Loader write-back could bake rows into it and duplicate inserts next boot.apps/cli/src/profile-boot.ts:194-200

Before boot, the launcher computes one immutable package table from the installation and the ordered bundle dependency graphs. It mounts that table as PluginPackages during host preparation, so plugins loaded from the profile or the installation see the same Cordis instance.apps/cli/src/profile-boot.ts:232-235

The patch list is flattened and cloned: bundle layers in order, profile patch, home patch, overlays. The root Include reads the empty YAML array, applies the patch list in memory, and creates the rows.vendor/include/src/index.ts:245-263

boot() installs the Loader, runs the launcher's prepare callback, mounts the root Include, waits for the Loader to settle, and audits activation.packages/boot/app-boot/src/index.ts:1200-1241 profileContext, the launch environment, PluginPackages, and cmdlineArgs are provided before any config-tree entry mounts. The hmr row, for example, is disabled by !ctx.get('profileContext'), so it can only be enabled if that service exists before its row is evaluated.

Row creation is not activation. The Loader imports and starts entries concurrently, and each fiber becomes active only when its inject requirements are present. agent-loop waits for its services; webserver waits for webStartup; web-startup waits for cmdlineArgs. A missing service leaves a fiber pending; when a provider appears, Cordis refreshes the dependent fiber and it can start.vendor/cordis/src/fiber.ts:611-623 Row order carries no load semantics; activation is service-availability driven.

boot() waits on the Loader's task list, which drains imports and lifecycle work.vendor/loader/src/config/tree.ts:35-49 A fiber held by a missing service has no pending task, so the wait can finish with that row still pending. The audit then classifies every inactive row: failed with an error, or pending with the missing service names.packages/boot/app-boot/src/index.ts:1042-1083 "Present in config" and "running" are different states.

The web profile adds a second readiness gate. web-runtime waits for the Loader, runs the required-entry audit again, checks that webServer and connection exist, and only then prints the dsh web: URL and opens the browser. The URL line is a readiness signal: supervisors and the browser act on it. A required failure or a boot-time disposal announces nothing.packages/bundle/web-app/src/index.ts:218-258

The launcher path is the same for all products; the profile chooses the bundle stack. The mode bundles differ by the rows they insert and by who owns process lifetime. The base bundle inserts agent-loop. Web adds webserver, web-runtime, modules, and connection. Headless adds headless-runner; SDK adds sdk-jsonrpc-server; ACP adds acp. The launcher returns after boot and leaves process lifetime to the mounted plugins: a one-shot runner exits, an stdio server serves until disconnect, and the web server keeps running.apps/cli/src/profile-boot.ts:264-270

Where the mechanism lives

Three files carry the composition logic. profile-boot.ts loads the profile, computes the resolution, composes the patch list, and calls boot(). app-boot/src/index.ts owns Loader mounting, settlement, the startup audit, and StartupError. app-boot/src/profile.ts owns profile discovery, bundle resolution, and composeEntries. The required set is the policy outside every product bundle:

Actual source, index.ts:951-960

TypeScript
const requiredStartupEntryIds = new Set<string>([
  'agent-loop',
  'webserver',
  'web-runtime',
  'modules',
  'connection',
  'headless-runner',
  'acp',
  'sdk-jsonrpc-server',
])

The list is global, not profile metadata. Required is checked only for entries that exist and are enabled. An absent id is ignored. Web can share a list that names headless-runner, acp, and sdk-jsonrpc-server because those rows are not in its tree.packages/boot/app-boot/src/index.ts:1153-1167 The list defines a usable DSH application in one place, and adding a product means adding its endpoint id there. That is a chosen coupling, not a property of plugin trees.

What fails, and who decides

A malformed root or overlay stops startup for every row. A module import error, a schema rejection, a throwing !!js expression, or a throwing apply() are localized to one row and judged by whether that row is required. A missing service is not an error while the row can wait; it is pending. An unhandled rejection or an uncaught exception from detached work is fatal regardless of the row's id, because resuming the failed operation is not safe.packages/boot/app-boot/README.md:98-113

At startup, a required failure disposes the whole tree and rejects with StartupError.packages/boot/app-boot/src/index.ts:1242-1249 An optional failure produces one warning and siblings keep running. A required row that is present but waiting for a service also stops startup. An optional row that is waiting warns and may start later. The fail-loud guard writes one labelled diagnostic, releases the terminal if the product owns it, and exits 1 without resuming.packages/boot/app-boot/src/index.ts:844-870

An optional provider failure can still prevent a required consumer from activating. The consumer is required, so startup stops. Policy is per row; the dependency graph is not.packages/boot/app-boot/README.md:113

HMR (hot module replacement) changes the failure contract. The base bundle enables dsh-hmr with root: [] when the launcher supplies profileContext; headless, SDK, and ACP disable the same row in their patches.packages/bundle/base/cordis.patch.yml:27-32 root: [] means no module watching by default: HMR watches the profile manifest and two user patch files, re-reads bundle layers, and applies configuration changes. Source watching is opt-in.packages/boot/hmr/README.md:27-34

A later reload does not repeat the required-startup audit or roll back the whole update. A valid edit applies; a malformed live patch is rejected and the running configuration stays; a changed or new failure rejects the reload and keeps siblings. The first gate judged the initial composition; the reload gate judges a delta. A running tree can survive a reload that a fresh boot would have failed.packages/boot/app-boot/README.md:96

Teaching model. The failure matrix collapses several schema, expression, and import cases into one row. The boot README distinguishes them.

The composer below lets you toggle bundle layers and add a failing plugin; the question to watch is which failure stops the boot and which leaves the tree running.

Interactive · 1

Which layer decides the boot outcome?

Toggle a missing Web layer or a failing optional plugin, then break a required entry. Watch composition turn into activation and failure policy.

Mechanism summary

Bundles and patches compose rows over an empty root. A required entry that is absent or disabled is ignored by the required audit; an enabled required entry that fails or stays pending can stop startup. An optional failure warns while siblings keep running. A later user patch replaces the whole config of the row it targets.

Teaching model: the controls simplify real timing and concurrency; the rules follow the pinned source. Sources: profiles and bundles   global required ids

What is required, chosen, or inherited

Some of this follows from the problem. A program assembled from parts needs composition data, stable row ids, dependency-driven activation, and failure classification. Without the first, parts cannot be replaced; without the second, patches cannot address them; without the third, boot order becomes a manual list; without the fourth, one optional plugin can take down a product.

Some is a project choice. The empty root is a choice. So is npm as the bundle format, whole-config replacement instead of a deep merge, one global required list instead of per-profile metadata, and config-only HMR on web.

Some is inherited. The code still removes a retired experimental bundle from old profiles and normalizes a legacy headless bundle tuple that also listed the web bundle.packages/boot/app-boot/src/profile.ts:197-210 sdk-minimal is a deliberate exception that became a compatibility surface: one bundle owns its tree, skips dsh-base, and still provides agent-loop and sdk-jsonrpc-server, which the global required list expects.packages/bundle/sdk-minimal/cordis.patch.yml:1-11 packages/bundle/sdk-minimal/cordis.patch.yml:135-138

The cost of composability

Whole-config replacement is the first cost. Every override restates every field it keeps. When a base default changes, an override that copied the old value keeps the old behavior without a warning. --dump-config prints the composed rows and names the layer that changed each one. It prints !!js expressions verbatim, so it shows the expression, not the value.

Row order is not activation order. Reading the YAML cannot tell you when a plugin starts. Debugging a missing capability means reading inject declarations and the pending list, not counting lines in a bundle.

The global required list couples app-boot to every product. A new server product must add its endpoint id in a package that does not own the server. The coupling is explicit and keeps "usable application" in one place, but it must change with the product set.

YAML is executable. A !!js expression evaluates against the plugin context, so a configuration review is partly a code review. --dump-config-schema imports each composed module, so run it only against trusted profiles.

HMR is not a transaction. It can leave some rows updated and some not, and it does not restore the previous composition after a failed replacement. A full rollback would require stopping work already in flight.

Skipping a bad bundle keeps boot moving but does not guarantee the remaining composition is usable. A skipped provider can leave a required consumer pending, and the audit then stops startup with a pending-service message.

What carries forward

If you build a smaller harness, copy four moves. Start with an empty root and give every part a stable id. Put composition in data that an operator can inspect and a later layer can override. Let activation follow service dependencies instead of a hand-written order. Declare which rows are essential, and exercise the failure path, because an optional row can still strand a required consumer.

Do not copy the full apparatus for one product with a handful of plugins. A fixed entry list is easier to read than four layers of patches. Whole-config replacement needs tooling and discipline. A global required list is overkill when one launcher serves one surface. HMR only pays for long-lived surfaces that operators reconfigure while they run.

The storefront request has still not run. But the tree that will handle it now exists: a loop from base, a session log from base, tools from base, a browser transport from web-app, all mounted over an empty file and audited before the URL printed. The next chapter follows the first prompt into that loop.

Part II · The Loop/Chapter 03

One Turn, Many Steps

The turn engine, its durable inbox, retries, cancellation, and recovery.

≈ 10 min read3 figures1 interactionSource 687f282e
In this chapter · 12 sections
  1. Where this sits
  2. The smallest model
  3. One inbox, two boundaries
  4. Opening a turn
  5. Running a step
  6. Retries are not steps
  7. Cancellation
  8. Failure recovery
  9. What ends a turn
  10. Trade-offs
  11. Source map
  12. What carries forward

A coding agent rarely answers in one model call. The failing-test request produces a read, an edit, a test run, then a summary. The user sees one request and one answer. The runtime sees four model requests, three tool batches, and a stream that can fail in the middle of any of them.

The runtime needs a unit that can hold all of that work together. It also needs boundaries where new input, cancellation, and policy can enter without corrupting the sequence. DeepSeek Harness uses three nested units: the turn, the step, and the attempt.

Where this sits

The turn engine is the narrow spine of the product. Boot composes the process (chapter 2). The session log records the turn (chapter 4). Prompt assembly and tools fill each step (chapters 5 and 6). This chapter sits at the center: how the driver accepts work, opens and closes units, and reacts when the model asks for action.

The smallest model

Suppose a harness has one queue of user input, one model, and one tool loop. Each new user message starts a fresh request. The loop repeats until the model emits no tools. This model has no place for input that arrives during a tool call, no distinction between a retry and a new request, and no durable boundary that survives a crash.

Now add the conditions a real harness faces:

  • Input can be an ordinary follow-up, a correction that should join the current work, or context that should wait silently.
  • A model stream can fail and be retried. A retry should not duplicate the user messages already admitted.
  • Tools can request another model call, or conclude the work themselves.
  • Cancellation must preserve what the user already saw and leave valid tool history.
  • The log needs boundaries that a reader can interpret after a crash.

These pressures produce three units.

A turn is one wake-to-quiescence unit. It opens before input is claimed and closes when nothing more is owed. It is the durable boundary for a user-visible interaction.

A step is one model request plus the tool calls it produces. A turn can contain many steps. A step owns one prompt assembly and one admitted user batch.

An attempt is one model stream within a step. A retry creates another attempt. A successful attempt settles as an assistant message. A failed or cancelled attempt can settle as a log-only attempt record without changing model history.

One inbox, two boundaries

The queue has two lanes. next-turn holds ordinary prompts that deserve their own turn. next-step holds input that belongs at the next step boundary inside the current turn.

The public methods are thin wrappers over those lanes:

  • followup() adds a next-turn message and wakes the driver.
  • steer() adds a next-step message and wakes the driver.
  • inject() adds a next-step message without waking. It becomes visible at the next step that starts for some other reason.

packages/core/agent-loop/src/agent.ts:154-173

At a turn boundary, the driver claims every pending next-step message plus exactly one queued follow-up. Between steps, it claims only next-step input. This gives steering a precise meaning: a correction can join the current turn, while a new request waits for its own turn. The claim is itself a durable mutation of the inbox projection, so a resumed session can reconstruct which messages were already consumed.

The inbox is not a UI convenience. It lives in session events and folds through a registered projection. Even a cold reader with no live Agent can see what input is pending. That matters to the browser and to a resumed process, both of which need to reconstruct state without holding the original objects.

packages/core/agent-loop/src/inbox.ts:26-65

packages/core/agent-loop/src/inbox.ts:103-114

Opening a turn

The failing-test request arrives as a follow-up. The driver's wake activates a loop, and the loop opens the turn:

Text
Teaching pseudocode
open turn
claim next-step input plus one next-turn message
assemble prompt and tools
ask pre-step policy what to enter
if rejected or first batch empty: close turn without a step
otherwise: enter steps until nothing is owed

Two decisions in that sketch need emphasis.

First, turn/start is written before the input is claimed. A turn can therefore exist with no step and no model call. If a listener rejects the step or an empty batch results, the turn still has a truthful boundary: it opened, nothing entered, it closed. That avoids inventing a turn later from a user message.

Second, the prompt is assembled before agent/pre-step, not after. The waterfall needs the assembled tool schemas and prompt to make a real decision. A listener can reject the proposed step, replace the messages, or declare that the step starts a new request series. The fallback path projects any runtime context registered since assembly.

packages/core/agent-loop/src/agent.ts:267-296

packages/core/agent-loop/src/agent.ts:298-360

Running a step

Once a step is accepted, the driver writes step/start. It then resolves the model route before admitting any model-visible input. This ordering is deliberate. The route can change through the agent/request waterfall, and the chosen adapter may support different prompt-update behavior. If cancellation arrives while the route is being resolved, neither the system prompt nor the user batch is committed.

After the route is bound, the first attempt does five things in order:

  1. Reconciles the rendered system prompt against the existing system/message surface nodes.
  2. Appends the accepted user messages, with runtime context inserted once at its owned position.
  3. Appends a request/header if none exists, the envelope changed, or a new request series begins, and request/context if the route metadata changed.
  4. Derives model history from the session log and freezes the request.
  5. Streams the bound prepared call.

The test scenario's first step looks like this:

The model streams a read request for src/cart.test.ts. The loop publishes live chunks and settles the assembled assistant message. It then writes tool/call for each requested call. The tool registry executes them and the loop appends model-ordered tool/result events. Because the batch ran tools, the step returns without a final turn reason. The turn loop claims the next step, and the model sees the tool results.

The same pattern repeats for the edit and the test run. On the last step, the model emits text and no tool calls. That step closes as completed. Since no next-step input is waiting, the driver runs agent/turn-stopping once, then writes turn/end with reason completed.

A steered message changes this shape. If the user types "also check the empty-cart case" while the edit is running, that message waits in next-step. After the edit step, the next boundary claims it along with any tool results. The turn continues with another model request. Steering does not open a second turn.

A follow-up sent at the same moment goes to next-turn. It waits until the current turn closes, then starts a separate turn. The distinction survives resume because both lanes are durable.

Retries are not steps

An adapter can fail after the request was logged, or after partial output. The driver settles the failed stream as assistant/attempt, then runs the agent/request-error waterfall. A listener may return { kind: 'retry' }. If it does, the driver makes another attempt inside the same step.

The retry reuses the assembled prompt and the admitted user batch. It refreshes runtime context, as a provider might resolve different facts, but it does not rerun prompt assembly or agent/pre-step. The user batch is not appended twice. This is the practical reason attempts exist as their own settled records: a step can contain several model calls, and the log must not pretend each one was a new turn.

packages/core/agent-loop/README.md:120

If no listener retries, the error becomes the turn's ending. The turn reason is error, carrying the structured provider failure when one exists. A model failure does not kill the loop; it fails the turn and leaves the agent available for later work.

Cancellation

Cancellation is cooperative and durable.

A call to agent.cancel(cause) aborts the active driver. By default it also clears both inbox lanes. Passing keepInbox: true aborts the active turn but preserves queued work for later. The abort cause is recorded in turn/end as a closed union of user, parent, hook, or disposed.

packages/core/agent-loop/src/agent.ts:175-181

Three cancellation paths need special care.

Cancellation during route resolution or pre-step. No system prompt or user batch has been committed. The turn closes as aborted, possibly with no step at all. Late steering is not silently re-enqueued as a new turn.

Cancellation during an assistant stream. The loop keeps the content the user already saw as an interrupted: true assistant message. That retained prefix becomes model history on a later request. If the stream produced no content, the attempt remains log-only.

Cancellation during tools. The scheduler stops starting new calls. Calls that already started are drained. Calls that never started receive a durable tool/call plus an ABORTED_BEFORE_DISPATCH error result, so the history still pairs every call with a result. If a started call finishes with a real failure, that result is retained.

These rules protect two different consumers. The user should not lose text that appeared on screen. The model should not receive an assistant tool call with no corresponding result. The log can contain both, because a tool result is a durable fact even when it says the tool never ran.

Failure recovery

An error can arrive from many places: prompt assembly, adapter selection, stream settlement, tool scheduling, or a result observer. The driver contains the failure at a boundary and closes the turn with the most specific reason it has.

If a step fails after assistant tool calls were recorded, the loop checks which calls lack results. For each one it appends a synthetic error result. A call that was recorded but never completed gets TOOL_OUTCOME_UNKNOWN. A requested call with no start record gets TOOL_NOT_STARTED. Both messages tell the model how to retry safely. A started dispatch is drained before the step closes.

The logging order is part of the recovery contract: tool recovery, then step/end, then turn/end with the error. A future request therefore sees a balanced step and can decide what to do next.

What ends a turn

The durable TurnEndReason union names the outcomes a reader must distinguish:

Reason Meaning
completed The model stopped asking, or a tool concluded the turn.
blocked A pre-step listener rejected the proposed input.
aborted An active driver was cancelled, with a recorded cause.
error The turn failed with a structured LlmFailure.
max-tokens At least one step hit its output ceiling; the reason stays sticky if a later step completes.
interrupted Repair closed a turn that crashed before its ending.
forked Fork construction closed a turn inherited mid-flight.

The last two reasons are never emitted by a live loop. They belong to repair and fork paths, which chapter 8 covers. Keeping them in the same union lets a reader interpret any stored log without guessing from a missing event.

There is no built-in turn budget. A model can keep calling tools, and a steering message can keep a turn open. The source names this as a limitation and points to agent/turn-stopping as the policy hook for a deployment that needs a bound. A runaway loop is a policy problem, not a hidden constant in the driver.

Trade-offs

The turn/step split has clear costs.

The driver holds the most intricate ordering in the product. Input is claimed before policy, but not committed until after route resolution. A step can contain multiple attempts. Tool calls can continue a turn without a new user message. Each of those choices prevents a specific corruption, and each adds a place where a reader has to know the sequence.

The log carries more boundary events than a simple chat transcript would need: turn/start, every step/start and step/end, attempts, and turn/end. The events are small, but they are not free. They buy replayable failure recovery and a UI that can show work in progress without inventing state.

The inbox is durable, which makes pending input inspectable and resumable, but it also means clearing a queue writes events. An in-memory queue would be simpler. It would lose the answer to "what was queued when the process died?"

The loop's containment is similarly deliberate. A tool error becomes a tool result, not a dead process. A provider error fails a turn, not the agent. That resilience makes failures visible in the session instead of disappearing into a crash report, at the cost of a longer event stream and more recovery code.

What carries forward

Treat the turn as the user-visible unit, the step as the model-call unit, and the attempt as the stream unit. Keep the boundaries durable, and make every cancellation leave a balanced history. Those rules make the rest of the system possible: a log that can be replayed, a UI that can show partial work, and a model that never receives half a tool exchange.

The next chapter opens the record these units write. It asks why the model's history is a projection, why the UI's transcript is a different projection, and what it takes to reconstruct a request from events alone.

Interactive · 1

How does one prompt become several steps?

Advance the request, inject steering, or cancel. Track the inbox, the open step, and the durable events that survive.

Mechanism summary

A turn opens before input is claimed and closes when nothing is owed. A step is one model request plus any tool calls it produces. Steering joins the next step boundary in the same turn; a follow-up waits for a later turn. Cancellation keeps delivered assistant text, drains started tools, and records a result for every skipped call.

Teaching model: the controls simplify real timing and concurrency; the rules follow the pinned source. Sources: input lanes and cancel   claim rules

Part II · The Loop/Chapter 04

The Log Is the Conversation

Events, surfaces, request reconstruction, fork, and two kinds of truth.

≈ 10 min read3 figures1 interactionSource 687f282e
In this chapter · 12 sections
  1. The problem with a message array
  2. Events, sequences, and the surface
  3. Append is a commit point
  4. Deriving model history
  5. What a request contains
  6. The failing test as a log
  7. Two kinds of truth
  8. Fork, not copy
  9. Failure paths
  10. Trade-offs
  11. Source map
  12. What carries forward

A chat application can keep an array of messages and append to it. Resume is a database read. A UI can render the array. This design survives until the agent acts on the world. Then the record must answer harder questions: which tool call produced which edit, what the model saw before the edit, why a retry did not duplicate the user's message, and what the conversation looked like before a summary replaced part of it.

DeepSeek Harness makes the session event log the durable record and treats message history as a projection. The log is not a chat transcript. It is a typed sequence of facts from which several different views can be derived: model history, a human transcript, a trace, a fork seed, or a browser timeline.

The problem with a message array

Start with the simplest durable model: a list of messages. The model request uses the list. The UI renders the list. Resume loads the list.

The model's stream then fails after sending half an answer. The list now contains partial assistant text. Should the next request include it? The user saw it, so yes. But the failed attempt also produced a provider error and usage information that should not appear as assistant prose. A retry might succeed and produce a second answer. Now the list needs a notion of attempts, and the UI needs to know which attempt is visible.

Tools create a sharper problem. The model emits a tool call, and the process crashes before execution starts. A later request must not include a tool call without a result. It also must not claim the tool ran. The record has to represent a third state: "requested, never dispatched."

Compaction creates a third. Older history needs to leave the model's context while remaining available for audit and for the human transcript. If the list is overwritten, evidence disappears. If it is not, the model's context keeps growing.

A message array answers one question. The session log answers all of these by recording facts and projecting views.

Events, sequences, and the surface

A session event has a type, a payload, a sequence number, and a timestamp. The payload must be lossless JSON. Events are appended one at a time. Sequence numbers are contiguous from zero, and an event never changes after it enters the log.

packages/core/session/src/index.ts:761-827

Five event types can produce model messages: system/message, developer/message, user/message, assistant/message, and tool/result. These are surface events. Every surface event must declare how it enters the ordered surface through a surfaceOp.

The surface is a list of event sequence numbers in model-visible order. A surface event either appends a new node or replaces an existing range. A replacement is a new event at a new log position, but it takes the old range's place in the surface. The shadowed events remain in the log. This is the mechanism that lets a summary or a rewritten tool result change what the model sees without destroying history.

packages/core/session/src/surface.ts:68-90

A projection turns a surface event into an LLM message. Some surface events project to no message. An empty assistant event can carry usage, for example when a step reaches its max-tokens ceiling; empty system, developer, and assistant nodes otherwise hold surface positions without adding a wire message.

Other events are log-only. They are durable but never reach the model. turn/start, step/start, request/header, inbox splices, approval audits, and assistant/attempt all belong here. Log-only does not mean unimportant. It means the event records a fact about the run rather than a message in the prompt.

Live notifications such as agent/assistant-stream are a third category. They are process-local, fast, and lossy by design. They let a browser render tokens before the attempt settles. They are not the replay source. A hard process loss before settlement leaves no durable attempt stream, while a settled message carries the exact compact stream that produced it.

Append is a commit point

Session.append() is a commit point. It snapshots and validates the payload, assigns the next sequence, freezes the event, and commits it. The validation rejects values that JSON cannot preserve losslessly: BigInt, cycles, Map, Set, class instances, functions, undefined, sparse arrays, and negative zero. A stateful getter cannot pass validation with one value and store another, because the snapshot pass reads each nested value once.

Observer failures after the commit are contained. The event is already in the log, so a broken listener cannot make the append look unsuccessful or prevent later listeners from seeing the event.

This commit rule matters for recovery. If the process dies before an append, the event does not exist. If it dies after the append, the event exists in memory and may or may not have reached storage. Chapter 8 covers the durability barrier. Here, the important part is that the in-memory log has a single, ordered acceptance point.

Deriving model history

The driver builds each request from the log. It does not keep a parallel conversation array as the source of truth.

deriveMessages() walks the current surface nodes, projects each node to a message, and caches the result. Appending a node is cheap: only new nodes are projected. A replacement or a plugin-owned message projection increments a content generation, which forces a rebuild from the surface. The returned array is a fresh snapshot, while the message objects themselves are shared and deep-frozen.

Text
Teaching pseudocode
derive_messages():
  if surface.content_generation changed:
    reset cache
  for seq in surface.nodes after cache position:
    message = project(log[seq])
    if message exists:
      append message to cache
  return a fresh array over cached messages

packages/core/session/src/index.ts:966-1005

The cache explains a performance choice. Rebuilding the whole history every token would waste work and break identity checks. Incremental projection keeps stable messages stable. Freezing them makes the request safe to share with an adapter and makes later mutation visible as a bug rather than a mystery.

A message projection is a plugin-owned, pure interpreter for an event that changes existing message content. It can alter content, but it cannot mint identities or reorder nodes. The persistence layer needs the owning projection definitions to replay those events. This is why the session package treats projection ownership as part of the event contract rather than a client-side rendering detail.

What a request contains

A model request is not "the log." It is a frozen object built at the step boundary from three pieces:

  • the latest request/header snapshot, holding the call configuration and tool schemas;
  • the current derived message history;
  • the tool history needed to reconstruct dynamic tool declarations.

The header is a full canonical snapshot of the non-history request envelope. It carries the provider and model config, adapter defaults, and tools. It deliberately does not carry the system prompt. The prompt is a system/message surface node, because it needs the same replacement, projection, and cache behavior as other model-visible content.

The loop writes a header on the first request, on a resume, when the envelope changes, and when an explicit request series begins. Otherwise it inherits the latest one. request/context records route facts separately: provider, model, context window, and the route's system-prompt update mode. It is diagnostic and admission metadata, not part of request reconstruction.

Every model-visible input therefore has a durable event. A tool schema that appears only in a header is still logged, because the header is logged. A system prompt is logged as a system node. A user message is logged before the request is dispatched. If a reader has the log and the current code, the request can be rebuilt.

There is an important limit to that claim. "Reconstructable" means the harness can recover the input it sent. It does not mean every provider reads that input identically. An adapter can add transport fields, transform content, or apply provider defaults. The request header logs call config, adapter-default markers, and tools; request/context logs the route's model and prompt-update mode. Retry policy, input modalities, and adapter transport fields stay outside the session log, so the provider remains an external system.

The failing test as a log

The scenario produces a log that looks roughly like this. Sequence numbers are teaching values, not a trace from a real session.

Seq Event Model-visible?
0 agent/inbox/spliced No
1 turn/start No
2 step/start No
3 system/message Yes
4 user/message Yes
5 request/header No
6 assistant/message Yes
7 tool/call (read test) No
8 tool/call (read source) No
9 tool/result Yes
10 tool/result Yes
11 step/end No

At seq 6, the assistant message contains both text and tool calls. The model-visible tool calls are part of the assistant message; the tool/call events provide durable call identity and inputs. The tool results at 9 and 10 cite their call events. The next step's request derives messages [system, user, assistant, result, result] plus any new runtime context.

The raw log also shows events that never enter the transcript, such as step/end. A UI that only uploaded model messages would be smaller. It would also lose the boundaries needed to explain why a tool ran and when the turn closed.

Two kinds of truth

A replacement can change the model's history without changing what a human saw. The session layer exposes this distinction directly. Append-origin surface events are the durable source material for a human transcript. Replacement events are model-only shadowing nodes.

That is not an accident of implementation. Compaction should not erase the conversation the user already read. A debugger should be able to see the original tool output even when the model received a pruned version. A fork can choose a boundary in the raw log and then close the inherited turn without pretending the original turn ended.

packages/core/session/src/surface.ts:79-98

The browser does not render the log as a flat chat list. It correlates durable events and live chunks into conversation contexts, then a target view such as Chat or Trajectory builds its own snapshot. The server, CLI, and browser can therefore show different presentations of one record without becoming separate runtimes.

Fork, not copy

A fork copies an inclusive prefix of the source log. It then appends a marker that separates inherited history from child-owned work. If the cut lands inside an open turn or step, fork construction appends synthetic closers with reason forked, including error results for unanswered calls. The child owns those closers; inheritedEventCount counts only the copied prefix.

packages/core/session/src/fork.ts:10-30

This is different from cloning a message array. The child has a valid append-only log whose first events happened in another session. The marker preserves that lineage, and the closers make the inherited prefix interpretable as a completed history. A resumed child can then append new work without rewriting the parent's log.

Failure paths

The log's failure model is mostly about refusal. Invalid JSON is rejected before commit. A surface event without a surface marker is rejected. A replacement must name a current range and every shadowed node. A tool result replacement may change only content. A developer message that adds a tool must reference an earlier header containing that definition. A system head can only be rewritten by a system message over exactly that node.

These rules keep the surface fold total. A corrupt event cannot leave the session with half a replacement. The cost is a strict append path with many validations, plus a persistence format that must preserve every event type the build understands.

There is one gap the append rules cannot close. A process can die after the stream settled in memory but before the settlement was flushed, or even before the settlement event was appended. The log then lacks the attempt. The UI may have shown tokens that are no longer recoverable. The source calls this out explicitly. Durable means flushed, not merely rendered.

Trade-offs

A typed append-only log is a strong choice for an agent. It provides replay, audit, fork, deterministic projection, and a shared factual base for several surfaces. It also imposes costs that a simpler chat state avoids.

Every new model-visible fact needs an event type and a projection rule. Every replacement needs validation against the current surface. Every consumer that wants derived state must either replay events or register a projection. The log grows with operational detail, and storage must preserve unknown-but-ignorable records across versions.

The surface indirection is another cost. A reader cannot treat event order as message order. Sequence numbers can move backward in surface position after a replacement. A tool result's position may shift. The API names this distinction with separate types: a SessionSeq identifies an event, while surface order identifies a message position.

The payoff is that the system has one answer to "what happened?" and several disciplined answers to "what did this consumer see?" That is the foundation the next chapters build on: context assembly chooses what to put on the surface, tools write results to it, and persistence carries it across process boundaries.

What carries forward

The useful abstraction is not "store messages." It is "store facts and define projections over them." A small harness can start with one projection and add more when a real consumer needs a different view. The discipline that matters is keeping model-visible input reconstructable and keeping replacement separate from deletion.

The next chapter takes the request side of this record. It explains how prompt sections, tool schemas, and runtime facts become surface nodes, why the system prompt is not a request field, and how that choice interacts with provider caches.

Every model-visible message comes from a surface event. A replacement is a new log event that takes an earlier surface position and shadows a range of nodes. Raw events and append-origin messages stay in the log. The human transcript can use those originals while the model reads the current surface.
