Part II · The Loop/Chapter 05

Context at the Right Address

Prompt assembly, system nodes, route capabilities, and provider caches.

≈ 12 min read3 figures1 interactionSource 687f282e
In this chapter · 9 sections
  1. Where this sits
  2. Three inputs, three addresses
  3. The first step
  4. The second step
  5. The placement decision
  6. Tool changes
  7. What it costs
  8. What transfers
  9. Source map

The failing-test turn reaches its second step with three kinds of prompt material already decided. The operating instructions come from prompt sections. The callable tools come from the tool registry. Runtime facts such as the working directory and approval policy come from session services. The first step sent all three with the request to read src/cart.test.ts and src/cart.ts; the second must send them again with both tool results.

If the harness stored the instructions in a system field on the request, the log would contain the conversation but not a model-visible input. A resume, fork, Web inspector, or second reader would have to recompute it from whatever plugins were mounted. Copying it into the log too would create two homes for one fact.

DeepSeek Harness avoids that split by making the prompt a message. The difficult part is placement. The prompt can change between steps: a plan-mode section enters, a skill loads, a policy switches. Rewriting the first message on every change discards the provider's cached prefix. Appending a later system message preserves the prefix only on a model that reads the latest system message anywhere in the conversation. The harness asks the route which behavior it supports, then writes the change at an address that route can honor.

Where this sits

This chapter follows assembly into request construction. Assembly runs during step admission, after the loop claims input and before request preparation. The resulting system message, runtime snapshot, and header are the last state the loop builds before dispatch. The chapter assumes the turn and step machine from chapter 3 and the log and surface split from chapter 4, and stops before compaction and execution.

Three inputs, three addresses

An assembly collects the model-facing prompt material from registered providers into three parts, plus interpolation variables. Prompt sections are named, ordered text contributions. Runtime contexts are named, ordered contributions that become a user-role snapshot rather than system text. Tool schemas are names, descriptions, and JSON schemas for arguments.

Assembly sends nothing. Its candidate holds section text with variables still unresolved, context text, and tool schemas in canonical order. Rendering turns the sections into one string and the contexts into one snapshot. The tools go to a different destination.

The surface is the ordered list of events that produce model messages. A surface node is one such event. A projection derives messages or message updates from those events. Derived history is the message list produced by folding the surface. A system node is a surface node holding a system/message. The request header is the logged envelope of call configuration and tool schemas. It is not a message and produces no wire message.

A provider-side KV cache stores attention key and value state for a token prefix, which a later request with the same prefix may reuse. The harness controls the bytes and their order; the provider controls whether the cache is shared and whether a request hits it. This chapter says "prefix reuse" for what the harness arranges, and "cache hit" only for a provider outcome.

A request series is a run of requests that extend the previous message list. A series start marks a boundary where earlier messages may have been replaced, so prefix reuse is not expected across it. A route is one provider and model pair registered to serve a call. In-history is a route capability: the model reads the latest system message at any position as the complete prompt in force. Consolidation is the opposite placement: rewrite the first system node and empty later active nodes.

The first step

The loop claims the user prompt, then assembles. Sections merge from global and agent scopes, with a scoped section shadowing a same-named global one. They sort by order, then by code-unit name. Order numbers are centrally allocated, from harness identity at -1000 through tool guidance to source at 10000 and the persona suffix at 10200 packages/core/system-prompt/src/index.ts:131-165. Rendering drops empty sections and joins the rest with blank lines packages/core/system-prompt/src/index.ts:290-295.

The tool registry contributes the visible schemas for this scope packages/core/tools/src/index.ts:850-861. The list sorts by name unless configuration supplies an explicit order with a <unlisted-tools> rest entry. Registration order is a plugin-load artifact, so the service replaces it with a deterministic order.

Runtime contexts sort by their own allocation. The working directory is marked required and literal, so it survives optional-context suppression and its braces are not interpolated packages/session/working-directory/src/index.ts:90-96. Approval policy is optional and can be suppressed. Several contexts render under one sentence that says the snapshot supersedes earlier snapshots.

The loop then runs the agent/pre-step waterfall, where a listener can reject or rewrite messages before admission packages/core/agent-loop/src/agent.ts:267-288. After that decision, step/start opens the step. Request preparation runs agent/request, resolves the exact adapter with prepareCall, and binds that adapter's capabilities. Only then does the loop decide where the prompt goes packages/core/agent-loop/src/agent.ts:400-442.

On the first step there is no system node. The projection appends one, before the user message, even when the rendered prompt is empty. The empty node reserves surface position zero so a later non-empty prompt can rewrite the head. A non-empty node holds one text block; an empty node holds none and projects to no wire message packages/core/session/src/surface.ts:120-152.

The runtime snapshot is appended as a user message after the claimed prompt. The placement is deliberate: it is current session fact, not stable instruction, so a policy or directory change never rewrites the system prefix.

Finally, buildRequest writes the envelope. The header holds the call config, any adapter-materialized defaults, and the assembled tools. It has no prompt field. The type makes that explicit with system?: never, and the session rejects a stored header that carries one packages/core/session/src/types.ts:241-252. The request carries the header's config, derived messages, tool declarations, tool history, sessionId, and abort signal.

Teaching model. This trace shows one assembly and one admitted request per step. In the implementation, a retry reuses the accepted assembly and re-projects it rather than reassembling. The storefront repository and its prompt sections are fictional teaching material.

The second step

The tool result is a new surface node. The prompt renders to the same bytes, and the assembled tools have the same names and definitions. The header equals the previous header, so no header event is appended. The projection finds the latest system node already holding the rendered text and emits nothing. The request extends the previous list with the assistant's tool call and its result.

This is the common case that prefix reuse depends on. An unchanged prompt costs no new prompt event. An unchanged tool set costs no new declaration. The runtime snapshot also stays unchanged unless a service reports a new fact. A shop whose directory, policy, and prompt are stable pays for the conversation rather than repeated assembly artifacts.

Now suppose an operator switches the approval policy between steps. The approval context text changes. The runtime projection compares the new snapshot with the retained one, appends a new user message, and leaves the system node alone. The approval service records the reason in a comment: the complete current value travels after retained history, so switching policy does not rewrite the stable system-prompt cache prefix packages/interaction/user-approval/src/index.ts:160-173.

The old snapshot remains, and the new one says it supersedes earlier copies. The cost is retained tokens; the benefit is that a short-lived fact never enters the long-lived prefix. A prompt change is different: it must alter what the model treats as instructions, so it needs a system node operation.

The placement decision

SystemPromptProjection scans the surviving system nodes on every projection. Its decision has three branches packages/core/agent-loop/src/runtime-context.ts:88-103:

Text
Actual source, runtime-context.ts:95-102
if (!input.inHistory || input.startsSeries || rendered.length === 0) {
  const updates = nodes.slice(1).filter(node => node.text !== '')
    .map(node => this.replace(node.seq, ''))
  if (head.text !== rendered) updates.push(this.replace(head.seq, rendered))
  return updates
}
if (latest.text === rendered) return []
return [{ message: createSystemMessage(rendered), intent: { surfaceOp: 'append' } }]

With no surviving system node, the projection appends one. This is the first-step branch.

When the route cannot read a later system message, or a series starts, or the rendering is empty, the projection consolidates. It first empties every non-empty later system node through a logged per-node replacement. Then it rewrites the head if its text differs from the rendering. The branch still normalizes the head and any later nodes when the latest prompt text matches.

On a continuing in-history series with a non-empty rendering, the projection appends only when the latest prompt text differs. An unchanged prompt emits nothing. The effective prompt is the last non-empty system node, falling back to the head. When the route declares systemPromptUpdate: 'in-history', the prepared call reports it, and the loop passes that fact into the projection packages/llm/llm/src/types.ts:408-425. The loop records the mode in a separate request/context event for readers when it changes, but admission uses the bound adapter rather than the latest logged snapshot packages/core/session/src/types.ts:397-403.

The built-in catalog shows both cases. At the pinned commit, deepseek-flash declares systemPromptUpdate: 'in-history' and toolUpdate: 'addition-only'. deepseek-v4-pro declares neither packages/llm/llm-deepseek/src/models.ts:5-20. A deployment can replace the catalog. The harness still trusts the prepared route declaration rather than inferring support from the model name.

A request series starts when the pre-step decision declares startsRequestSeries or when the surface generation changed since the last request. A visible tool change on a route without toolUpdate also forces prompt consolidation; if that consolidation replaces a system node, the resulting surface generation starts a new series. A provider swap alone does not start one; prefix reuse is not expected, and a capable destination can append.

An empty rendering always consolidates, regardless of route or series. The head becomes empty, and every non-empty later system node is emptied through a replacement that cites the shadowed node. No older instructions remain model-visible. Repeated clears add no events, because the head is already empty and no later node is non-empty. The admission spec exercises this on both capable and plain routes, including a seeded resume and a later restore packages/core/agent-loop/tests/system-prompt-admission.spec.ts:178-215.

The surface fold protects node zero. A replacement that covers node zero while that node is a system message must itself be a system message over exactly that node packages/core/session/src/surface.ts:493-507. Later system nodes have no such protection, which is what lets a compaction replacement shadow them. That boundary is where this chapter stops.

The comparator below asks which prompt placement a route can support and what cache prefix survives a change.

Interactive · 1

Where should a changed prompt live?

Choose a route capability and a prompt change. Watch where the system node moves and which request prefix can still be reused.

Mechanism summary

On a continuing route that reads the latest system message in history, a changed non-empty prompt appends after the retained history, so earlier tokens can remain reusable. A route without that capability, a new request series, or a clear consolidates at the system head. An empty rendering clears every active system node.

Teaching model: the controls simplify real timing and concurrency; the rules follow the pinned source. Sources: prompt projection   request header and route metadata

Tool changes

Tools take the other address. The header records the assembled schemas, and header equality compares config, adapter defaults, and the ordered tool list, including each schema's JSON packages/core/session/src/request-header.ts:43-52. Adding, removing, reordering, or redefining a tool therefore changes the header. On a later request, when the set of names changes, buildRequest appends one developer message listing the additions and removals. Additions cite the new header so an offline reader can resolve the definition packages/core/agent-loop/src/agent.ts:652-666.

Route capability matters here too. A route without toolUpdate receives the complete current list and no developer update messages packages/llm/llm/src/content.ts:430-436. A route with addition-only or in-history can defer an added declaration and activate it from history. in-history also reads removal blocks; addition-only cannot deactivate a tool through history, so a removal still changes the declaration list.

Prompt placement interacts with tool capability here. On a route without toolUpdate, a visible tool change forces prompt consolidation even when the prompt text is unchanged. The declaration prefix is already broken, so retaining a second prompt version buys no cache and costs tokens. The reconstruction spec exercises a changed header that starts a series and folds the prompt back into node zero packages/core/agent-loop/tests/request-reconstruction.spec.ts:723-743.

A same-name definition change modifies the header without changing the name set. No developer addition or removal is emitted. The full declaration list changes, so the prefix differs from the first altered schema token.

What it costs

The design buys one representation for model-visible prompt text. Every reader folds the same surface, and a request can be reconstructed from the log without running the prompt plugins again. A prompt change and a tool change are also distinguishable: the former is a system node operation, the latter a header change with optional developer notices.

Retained prompt versions. On an in-history route, appended system nodes stay in history. Every later request in the series pays for the old versions until a replacement or compaction shadows them. A deployment whose prompt changes on most steps should move that fact into runtime context instead.

Cache dependence on the route. Consolidation that rewrites node zero makes the request differ from its first token. In-history appends keep the prefix but depend on the model contract. A proxy that rewrites or reorders system messages can break the contract without any local error. The harness can record the declared capability; it cannot verify that a remote service honors it.

Tool declarations in the prefix. Schemas are part of the cached prefix. Deferring an addition helps, but changing a retained definition still invalidates reuse from the first altered declaration. Tool order must be canonical for the same reason: a plugin-load order that leaked into the request would make identical assemblies look different.

Runtime snapshot growth. A changing fact is appended rather than rewritten. That keeps the prompt prefix stable and lengthens history with superseded snapshots. The model is told the latest snapshot supersedes earlier ones, but the tokens remain.

Loud assembly failures. An unknown name in toolOrder, a malformed or unresolved variable, or two sections that both claim the whole prompt all throw before a request is sent. A plugin misconfiguration surfaces at the first model step, not at boot.

Cancellation leaves no half-request. If cancellation lands during agent/request or prepareCall, the loop commits neither the system prompt, nor the user messages, nor a header. A reader cannot find a prompt for a request that never went out.

What transfers

Copy the separation of addresses. Keep one durable representation for text the model treats as instructions, and put declarations in the envelope. A request field is a poor home for a fact that must be replayed, because replay then depends on live code rather than the log.

Separate facts by lifetime. Stable identity, policy prose, and tool guidance belong in the prompt. Directory, endpoint, policy mode, and other session facts belong in a late snapshot that changes without rewriting the prefix. If a fact changes often, this split matters more than the prompt text.

Make placement a property of the route. A deployment flag can pair a model with a representation it does not understand. The route that will serve the call should declare whether it reads a later system message, and the loop should decide after binding that route.

Log the operations as well as the result. A replacement cites the node it shadows; a tool addition cites the header that defines it. Clearing replaces every active version instead of appending an empty one, so an older prompt cannot become effective again. These choices make offline reconstruction possible without a second prompt store.

Do not copy the design when the constraints are absent. A single-process tool with no resume, no fork, no alternate reader, and one static prompt can pass a system string on each request and be simpler. A system that changes its prompt constantly may do better by moving the changing text into runtime context. The design earns its complexity when the log must explain what the model saw and when the provider prefix is worth protecting.

The next chapter follows the tool calls this request declares into execution. The prompt has reached the model as a message; the tools are about to touch the world.

Part II · The Loop/Chapter 06

Tools at the Edge of the World

Canonical tool values, scoped visibility, policy, concurrency, and results.

≈ 11 min read4 figures1 interactionSource 687f282e
In this chapter · 12 sections
  1. Where this sits
  2. The tool contract
  3. The definition
  4. What an agent can see
  5. The execution pipeline
  6. Failure becomes a result
  7. Ordering and concurrency
  8. Cancellation and recovery
  9. The failing test
  10. Trade-offs
  11. Source map
  12. What carries forward

The failing-test request becomes real when the model asks to read a file, then edit it, then run a command. Everything before that point manipulates text. A tool call changes the machine.

That change creates a different kind of engineering problem. Model output is untrusted input. A tool can be slow, concurrent, or destructive. Its arguments must be validated, its result must be recorded in the same order the model requested it, and cancellation must not leave a tool call without an outcome. A failed tool should usually become information for the model, not kill the run.

DeepSeek Harness handles this with a tool definition, a scoped tool registry, and a fixed execution pipeline. The definition says what a capability is. The registry decides what a given agent can see. The pipeline decides whether a call may run and what result becomes durable.

Where this sits

The loop schedules tool calls after an assistant message (chapter 3). The model sees tool schemas assembled into each request (chapter 5). This chapter covers the path from the model's proposed call to a durable tool/result. Approval and sandboxing enter the pipeline as policy; chapter 7 explains those decisions. Here, the question is how the pipeline gives policy a place to act without making every tool a policy implementation.

The tool contract

Suppose the interface is a function and a JSON schema. The registry sends the schema to the model, parses the arguments, and calls the function. That covers the happy path.

Now add the conditions the source treats as part of the contract:

  • Arguments must be validated and frozen so a policy listener cannot see one value while the body receives another.
  • The successful return value must have a declared shape. Otherwise a tool can silently produce content the UI or a programmatic caller cannot interpret.
  • Model-facing content is not always the same as the canonical value. A terminal result, a diff, or a read window needs a presentation projection that can be replayed without the original process.
  • The tool may be offered to one agent and hidden from another.
  • Concurrent calls can overlap only when the tool explicitly says it is safe. Everything else must be a barrier.
  • Cancellation must distinguish "never started" from "started and may have had side effects."
  • A failure must become a structured error result without necessarily ending the turn.

These requirements produce the tool contract.

The definition

A tool definition has a model-facing name, description, and parameter schema; a canonical output declaration with a JSON schema and a renderer; and an execute() body. Optional callbacks add concurrency classification, deferred content projection, final content transformation, and presentation metadata.

defineTool() compiles the author-facing schema DSL into JSON Schema, validates arguments before the body, and wires the callbacks. The output declaration is mandatory, including for raw registrations. The registry rejects a definition without it.

packages/core/tools/src/index.ts:1065-1079

packages/core/tools/src/schema.ts:554-631

Two distinctions inside the definition matter throughout the pipeline.

The canonical value is the tool's real return value. It is lossless JSON, validated against output.schema, and available to a programmatic caller. The rendered content is what the model reads. output.render(args, value) produces content blocks. A policy can replace the model-facing content without changing the canonical value available to a parent program; a policy that must deny programmatic access has to block or replace the value too.

The presentation is a third surface, for humans. presentCall() and presentResult() describe a card, and presentationMeta() derives durable metadata from the canonical value. The Web client does not consume these Host presentation methods directly. It derives its own card from raw events and persisted metadata, with a generic fallback. The separation matters because a UI can replay a tool card after the tool code has changed, without the original process.

What an agent can see

The registry stores tools in layers. A global layer holds composition-wide tools. An agent-scoped layer holds tools registered through that agent's context. Scope chains allow a child or nested context to inherit from its parents.

The visible set is resolved in one pass:

  1. Start with global tools, nearest ancestor last.
  2. Apply restrictions from every layer in the scope chain. Restrictions intersect, so any ancestor can mask an inherited tool.
  3. Add the scope's own registrations. They shadow inherited names and are exempt from restrictions on what the scope inherits.
  4. Insert the run_code transport if the scope's presentation mode needs it.

The exemption for the scope's own registrations is not a loophole. It lets a delegation runtime register a structured-output tool in a child's own layer without having the child's capability filter strip the machinery that reports the result. The restriction still applies to everything the child inherits.

The model-facing schemas are a whitelist projection. They keep the name, description, parameter schema, and an optional deferred-loading marker. Callbacks, timeout budgets, concurrency classifiers, and presentation code stay host-side.

packages/core/tools/src/index.ts:1186-1226

The execution pipeline

The pipeline has seven stages. Some are extensible waterfalls, some are fixed by the registry, and one is an observation-only notification.

1. Materialize and freeze the call. The registry snapshots the parsed arguments as lossless JSON, assigns an opaque execution token, captures the finalizer and content projector, and freezes the identity fields. The call is now safe to hand to policy code.

2. tools/pre-execute waterfall. Listeners may allow, deny, cancel, or ask. A listener owns the decision by returning it; next() delegates. This is where hooks, permission rules, and external policy adapters attach.

3. Approval and guards. An ask decision is resolved through ctx.approval. If no answerer can decide, the call is denied. After the waterfall, registered guards run. A guard can only deny. It cannot turn a previous denial back into permission, so ordering cannot weaken a monotonic policy.

4. tools/execute waterfall. Wrappers can impose a timeout, retry, retry bookkeeping, or metrics. They receive a dispatch view with a replaceable signal, but they cannot remove the caller's cancellation. The registry fuses the caller signal back before the body.

5. The body. execute(args, exec) performs the action. It must observe exec.signal and settle only after its owned work quiesces. The registry cannot hard-kill same-process code, which is why the contract is cooperative.

6. Content projection and tools/post-execute. The tool's projectContent can install execution-prepared content before policy. Then post-execute listeners may accept, replace content or value, block the result, or attach model-facing context. Definition-owned finalizeContent runs last and may change only content.

7. Materialize the final result and notify. The result is snapshotted, frozen, and passed to tools/result observers. The loop then writes the durable tool/result with the call's sequence as a source reference.

packages/core/tools/src/index.ts:1497-1544

packages/core/tools/src/index.ts:1649-1722

packages/core/agent-loop/src/tool-calls.ts:278-291

The split between steps 2 and 3 is deliberate. The waterfall is reorderable and extensible. Guards are monotonic. A deployment can install a policy plugin with prepend and still keep a final owner guard that no later plugin can undo. The cost is two places to look when a call is denied; the benefit is that policy composition has a defined ceiling.

Failure becomes a result

Most tool failures do not throw out of the executor. They become an isError result.

A denied call produces a model-facing error reason and optional structured failure info. A thrown body becomes an error result. Invalid arguments, a non-JSON return, a schema mismatch, a throwing renderer, or a failing content finalizer all become normalized errors before observers run. An unknown tool is a structured UNKNOWN_TOOL failure. A cancellation before the body starts produces ABORTED_BEFORE_DISPATCH; a cancellation after a successful body produces ABORTED, while a tool-owned failure is preserved.

This normalization is what lets the agent loop stay a loop. The model reads a failed result and can repair its arguments, choose another tool, or explain the problem. A tool failure is usually information. The exceptions are scheduler failures or failures in the recovery machinery itself, which close the step.

The result also carries privacy boundaries. A failure may include structured error.info for the host, while model content gets only a safe message. A post-execute block can discard a result and replace it with corrective feedback. Those choices belong to policy, not to the tool author's error text.

Ordering and concurrency

The model can request several calls in one assistant message. The loop does not run them all concurrently. It classifies each call from the live registry:

  • parallel only when the definition's isConcurrencySafe(args) returns exactly true;
  • exclusive for a missing classifier, false, a thrown classifier, a truthy non-boolean, or an unknown tool.

The scheduler consumes the calls in model order. An exclusive call is a barrier: it runs alone. A run of parallel calls forms a bounded pool, with a default limit of 10. Later calls are reclassified after earlier completions, so a registry change can create a new barrier. Dispatch bodies may overlap, but pre-execute policy and result commits stay in model order.

The result-order rule prevents a fast second call from racing ahead of a slow first call in the transcript. The model asked for calls in one order. Its next request should see the outcomes in that order. The canonical result also becomes durable, frozen, and linked to its call.

The concurrency classifier is an opt-in safety claim. A tool author says, in effect, "for these arguments, this body can overlap with siblings without violating its own state." The default is exclusive because the registry cannot infer that property. This is a limitation as well as a safety choice: a tool whose safety depends on comparing sibling calls cannot express that relation in a unary classifier, so it must stay exclusive.

Cancellation and recovery

Cancellation has three states with different evidence.

Cancelled before start. The call is recorded with the model-visible result ABORTED_BEFORE_DISPATCH. No body ran, so retrying is safe from the harness's perspective.

Cancelled after start. The scheduler stops starting new calls and waits for started dispatches to settle. A successful result that arrives after cancellation is replaced with ABORTED; a tool-owned error is kept. The history does not claim the call had no effect.

Step failure. If the step throws after some assistant calls were recorded, the loop records recovery results for calls without outcomes. A call that started but did not finish gets TOOL_OUTCOME_UNKNOWN; a call with no start record gets TOOL_NOT_STARTED. The recovery text tells the model to retry read-only or idempotent work and to verify external state before retrying a side-effecting call.

packages/core/agent-loop/src/tool-calls.ts:146-246

The cancellation path is why the call is logged before the body. The tool/call event is evidence that the model asked, even if the tool never ran. The corresponding result can then distinguish "never started" from "started and unknown." Without the call log, both states collapse into a missing result.

The failing test

The model requests two reads in one assistant message: the test file and src/cart.ts. Both definitions declare safe reads, so the scheduler starts them together. The second read finishes first, but its result waits in its model-order slot. The first finishes and both results commit in order.

The edit arrives in the next assistant message, after the model has seen those results. It is an exclusive call, so it runs alone. The test command arrives after the edit and is also exclusive. Within the first batch, the two reads overlap; across batches, each step starts only after the previous step's results are durable. The same scheduler handles both cases.

For a batch that mixes modes, an exclusive call acts as a barrier behind any parallel pool. The model asked for calls in one order, and their outcomes should reach its next request in that order. A fast second call cannot jump ahead of a slow first call in the transcript.

If the user cancels during the test command, the reads and edit remain in the log. The test call is already started, so it drains. If it returns successfully after the abort, the result becomes ABORTED. The model's next turn sees the edit's result and an aborted test, so it does not assume the tests passed.

Trade-offs

The pipeline is long, and most tools do not need every stage. A small system can collapse several stages and still preserve the core properties: validate and freeze input, put policy before side effects, normalize failures into results, and log the call before dispatch.

The canonical-output requirement adds authoring work. A tool that wants to return arbitrary prose must declare a value, a renderer, and optionally presentation metadata. The payoff is a stable API for programmatic callers and replayable UI, but it makes tool authoring more demanding than returning a string.

The scoped registry is more complex than a global map. It supports per-agent capability sets and child filters, but it also means "is this tool available?" depends on the viewing agent and the live registry state. The debug answer is a resolved view for that scope, not a global list.

The pipeline's failure containment has a cost in diagnosis. A denied or failed call looks the same at the top level (an error result), and the detailed reason lives in policy listeners, failure metadata, or logs. The source keeps structured error info beside the model content for this reason, but a caller still needs to know which stage produced the result.

The concurrency model is conservative. It leaves performance on the table when a tool could be parallel for some arguments but has no classifier, and it cannot express sibling-dependent safety. The default is safe. The model may wait longer than an idealized scheduler would.

Interaction assumption. The tool lab uses a three-call batch and a 10-call concurrency limit to keep the timeline legible. It does not model provider latency, filesystem caching, or approval answer time. The pipeline order and result rules follow the pinned source.

What carries forward

A tool call is a small protocol: validate input, decide permission, execute, normalize, persist, and report. The protocol outlives any individual tool. Once it exists, a read, a shell command, and an MCP call can share the same safety and recovery rules.

The next chapter follows the permission decision itself. It asks when the harness should ask a human, what a grant authorizes, and how a sandbox turns a policy into an operating-system boundary.

Mechanism summary

A tool call is logged before its body runs. Pre-execute may allow, deny, ask, or cancel. An ask resolves through the approval seam and fails closed. Guards can only deny. A denied or failed call becomes a model-visible error result; cancellation before dispatch is marked ABORTED_BEFORE_DISPATCH, while a started call drains and may produce ABORTED.

Part III · Trust and Time/Chapter 07

A Gate, Not a Vibe

Approval, fail-closed outcomes, sandbox modes, and honest enforcement.

≈ 11 min read4 figures1 interactionSource 687f282e
In this chapter · 9 sections
  1. The smallest model
  2. Consent is not capability
  3. The edit that is refused
  4. One grant, one call
  5. The test that runs in a wrapper
  6. Where the checks live
  7. When the platform keeps only part of the promise
  8. The execution world behind the policy
  9. What transfers

The failing discount test needs one edit. The agent has read src/cart.test.ts and src/cart.ts, and now calls edit with a new total calculation. Before the bytes reach disk, two questions have to be answered: may this exact call proceed, and what may the writing process touch if it does? The first belongs to the approval seam. The second belongs to the process sandbox, a file-effect policy wrapped around a spawned command or applied to a filesystem mutation. Neither layer answers the other's question.

This chapter follows that call to the operating system and back. The repository is teaching material.

The smallest model

An approval is a same-process permission question about one action. It carries the agent, tool name, and usually the tool-call id, but not the arguments: the answerer attaches its prompt to the tool call already shown. The answer is a closed outcome, not a boolean. The source defines exactly four values packages/interaction/user-approval/src/types.ts:28-32:

TypeScript
/**
 * Closed approval outcomes: a one-shot grant, explicit rejection, withdrawn
 * request, or unavailable answerer. Callers fail closed on `unavailable`.
 */
export type ApprovalOutcome = 'allowed-once' | 'rejected' | 'cancelled' | 'unavailable'

allowed-once is the only grant. rejected means a human or a policy said no. cancelled means the request was withdrawn, usually through its abort signal. unavailable means no usable answerer produced a decision. Treating unavailable as permission inverts the contract.

A sandbox here is narrower than the word suggests. It is a policy over file effects, expressed as a mode and a workspace root, applied either by a sandboxed subprocess runner or by an in-process filesystem fence. The modes are read-only, workspace-write, and danger-full-access packages/sandbox/sandbox/src/index.ts:24-33. read-only denies writes apart from a required sink such as /dev/null; workspace-write adds the workspace and platform temp areas; danger-full-access bypasses the provider.

Enforcement is a reported fact about a backend, not a fourth mode. full means the backend governs every promised file effect. partial means an active backend or an older kernel interface governs only a subset packages/sandbox/sandbox/src/index.ts:55-60. Approval and sandbox are seams; the mode policy is shared core, which lets consent and confinement evolve independently.

Consent is not capability

Approval answers a question about intent. The service records an audit entry, asks the composed answerer chain, and returns one of four outcomes. It never runs the tool and never widens a boundary. Sandboxing answers a question about capability. It wraps an argv or checks a target path, and it has no notion of who consented or why. A sandbox cannot ask a human, and an approval cannot stop a process from opening a file after the answer returns.

A sandbox denial can become a question; a grant becomes a wider per-call policy. The tool runs again under that policy, and the sandbox enforces the boundary. Approval is the reason to try a wider mode; the sandbox makes it mean something.

The base composition mounts both layers: the local sandbox provider, a workspace-write policy rooted at the process cwd, the sandboxed bash executor, approval at ask, and presets pairing read-only and workspace-write with ask and danger-full-access with never packages/bundle/base/cordis.patch.yml:238-276.

The edit that is refused

Reads pass in every mode. The session here is pinned to read-only. The sandboxed filesystem leaves reads untouched and fences only writeText and editText packages/fs/fs-sandbox/src/index.ts:6-8. When the agent calls edit, the tool resolves the complete policy before touching the file. The resolver prefers an explicit approved mode, then the session's last sandbox/mode event, then the deployment default, and it takes the workspace root from the session's immutable cwd packages/sandbox/sandbox-policy/src/index.ts:164-171.

Under read-only, the provider refuses with a structured FS_SANDBOX_DENIED before any write packages/fs/fs-sandbox/src/index.ts:122-144. The tool maps it to [sandbox: file access denied under read-only mode] plus an offer to retry once with sandbox_permissions and a justification.

The retry is not a quiet mode change. The tool checks that the two escalation arguments travel together and that the justification is a non-empty sentence, then compares the requested and effective modes. The ladder is strict: read-only may escalate to workspace-write or danger-full-access; workspace-write may escalate only to danger-full-access; nothing escalates to read-only packages/sandbox/sandbox/src/escalation.ts:22-31. Repeating the effective mode succeeds without asking.

For a genuine widening, approveEscalation requires an approval service and an agent. It builds an audit reason naming the target mode and the model's justification, asks for one decision, and maps the outcome packages/sandbox/sandbox/src/escalation.ts:171-207. On allowed-once it returns the requested mode. On rejected, cancelled, or unavailable it throws a distinct error before anything executes.

The service requires an open turn, mints a fresh ApprovalRequestId, appends approval/asked, obtains one outcome, appends approval/decided, and returns it packages/interaction/user-approval/src/index.ts:215-234. Both events are log-only: durable and replayable, but not in the model transcript and carrying no surfaceOp packages/interaction/user-approval/src/types.ts:34-59.

The open-turn rule protects the replay boundary that crash repair understands. The approval service refuses to create an audit pair outside a turn rather than write events that no replayable execution encloses. Persistence itself does not discard between-turn events; the refusal is the approval service's decision.

The answerer chain is a waterfall: each listener may return an outcome to claim the single slot or call next() to pass. No answer yields unavailable. A throwing answerer becomes unavailable, a non-vocabulary return is normalized to it, and an abort settles cancelled while a late answer is discarded packages/interaction/user-approval/src/index.ts:267-307.

The policy sits in front. ask delegates to the answerers; never returns rejected inside the service before any listener runs. A gate implemented as a listener could be bypassed by Cordis prepend order, so a test prepends an eager grant after mount and asserts it is never consulted packages/interaction/user-approval/tests/approval.spec.ts:430-442.

The effective policy is the last approval/policy event, falling back to configuration packages/interaction/user-approval/src/index.ts:243-259. Sandbox mode has the same shape: one log-only sandbox/mode event, folded and replayed packages/sandbox/sandbox-policy/src/session-mode.ts:24-38. Policy survives a restart; a grant does not.

One grant, one call

The service holds no grant table; it returns a value. One-shot is a property of how the consumer uses that value, not a durable permission.

Teaching pseudocode: one escalated call

Text
standing = policy.resolve(session)            // read-only
if args.sandbox_permissions and args.justification:
    target = narrowest_wider(standing.mode, args.sandbox_permissions)
    outcome = approval.request(call_id, reason, target)
    if outcome is not allowed-once: stop with the outcome-specific error
    policy = { ...standing, mode: target }    // stamped on this call only
else:
    policy = standing
result = run_confined(argv, policy)

The edit tool follows that shape: resolve the standing policy, validate the arguments, ask if a widening is requested, and return a policy whose mode is approved. The filesystem provider receives that object for one mutation packages/fs/tool-fs/src/sandbox.ts:87-108. The next edit starts from the standing mode and asks again. Bash has the same structure: resolve, approve if present, stamp the approved mode onto the shell request packages/shell/tool-bash/src/index.ts:478-497.

The tool-call id ties the question to the visible action, so the answered prompt attaches to the tool call the user already saw. The approval id pairs the two audit events.

never still writes the audit pair: the log records that the harness asked and that the outcome was rejected. That separates an absent answerer from a policy or human rejection.

The test that runs in a wrapper

For bash, the tool passes the command and per-call policy to the shell seam. For a confining mode the executor calls ctx.sandbox.confine with the exact argv it is about to spawn, here ['bash', '-c', command] packages/shell/bash-sandbox/src/index.ts:89-132. The provider returns a replacement argv, enforcement fact, denial dialect, and runner rules; the executor spawns it and keeps the facts until settlement.

The provider chooses a runner by platform. Linux tries bwrap before Landlock, macOS uses Seatbelt, and Windows uses the ACL restricted-token runner packages/sandbox/sandbox-local/src/index.ts:160-167. A sole candidate needs no probe; a multi-candidate chain is arbitrated by one; no usable candidate fails closed packages/sandbox/sandbox-local/src/index.ts:509-520.

The executor reports what happened, not what was requested. A nonzero exit whose stderr matches the active backend's denial dialect becomes denied. On a foreground call, a fatal runner line becomes SandboxUnavailableError: the command did not run, so it is an infrastructure failure, not a failing test. A settled background process carries runnerFailed instead. Runner failure is checked first because a runner error can contain denial words packages/shell/bash-sandbox/src/index.ts:115-131.

The model marker is the same vocabulary the filesystem uses. A denied bash file effect produces [sandbox: file access denied under workspace-write mode], with the escalation hint when the composition advertises it. The marker names the mode because the same command can fail differently under a different policy.

If the test writes a cache outside the workspace, the model can retry once with danger-full-access and a justification. The grant is again one call, and under the default ask policy the user sees the prompt. The executor then skips the provider and spawns the original argv; no enforcement fact is reported because nothing confined it.

Where the checks live

A tools/pre-execute listener can return ask for any tool before monotonic guards run. The registry resolves it through ctx.approval and maps it one-to-one: allowed-once allows, and the three non-grants deny with distinct reasons. A missing service or agent-less call denies without asking. Cancellation that coincides with caller cancellation becomes the canonical abort result, not a policy denial packages/core/tools/src/index.ts:1507-1526 packages/core/tools/src/index.ts:1725-1775.

The sandbox escalation path is the second consumer. It lives inside the enforcing tool family, which alone knows the call id, effective mode, and denial subject. It uses the same service and union, mapping the grant to a mode.

The provider is the third checkpoint: ctx.sandbox.confine must return an enforcing argv or reject with SANDBOX_UNAVAILABLE; silent unconfined passthrough is forbidden packages/sandbox/sandbox/src/index.ts:153-177. A fourth is the consumer's classification: bash decides denial versus runner failure from the returned dialect, and the filesystem maps FS_SANDBOX_DENIED to the shared marker packages/fs/tool-fs/src/sandbox.ts:124-130.

When the platform keeps only part of the promise

The first failure is an absent decision. With no answerer, the service returns unavailable and the registry denies. A test with no listener gets an asked and a decided event whose outcome is unavailable packages/interaction/user-approval/tests/approval.spec.ts:63-75; a throwing transport is contained the same way packages/interaction/user-approval/tests/approval.spec.ts:253-259.

The second failure is a withdrawn question. An abort before the ask settles it as cancelled without consulting anyone; an abort during the ask discards the late answer. The test asserts one approval/decided event with cancelled even after the answerer later tries to grant packages/interaction/user-approval/tests/approval.spec.ts:289-305.

The third failure is an absent backend. confine throws SandboxUnavailableError with code SANDBOX_UNAVAILABLE; the command never runs. The text tells the operator to install a runner or switch to danger-full-access, an explicit composition choice rather than a silent fallback packages/sandbox/sandbox/src/index.ts:125-145. A late runner failure becomes the same error, not an ordinary task result packages/shell/bash-sandbox/tests/sandbox.spec.ts:603-610.

The fourth failure is partial enforcement. The local provider reports partial for the Windows ACL runner because hard links alias files across paths, reads remain unconfined, and some AppContainer ACLs are unreadable to the child. It also reports partial when the Landlock probe finds an older ABI packages/sandbox/sandbox-local/src/index.ts:536-539 packages/sandbox/sandbox-local/tests/local.spec.ts:322-326. A consumer needing the absolute promise must surface or reject it. Bash carries it through unchanged packages/shell/bash-sandbox/tests/sandbox.spec.ts:533-537. PTC prints a warning packages/core/tools/src/ptc.ts:370-374, but the ordinary bash renderer does not, so a direct bash call can leave enforcement outside the model-facing text. That is a presentation gap, not a sandbox property.

The fifth failure is a category error. The filesystem fence is a policy check in trusted code over a model-controlled path. It canonicalizes the target and checks containment immediately before the mutation, but it is containment, not a kernel boundary, and it accepts a narrow time-of-check window packages/fs/fs-sandbox/src/index.ts:10-18. Bash is the OS-level path. The filesystem fence and the macOS Seatbelt profile share a writable-root helper, while bwrap and Landlock keep their own grant spellings packages/sandbox/sandbox/src/roots.ts:43-54.

The sixth failure is scope. Mode and enforcement cover file effects; network access and process visibility are outside the vocabulary. Approval can gate a network tool through ask, but no sandbox promise backs that gate.

A final cost is message precision. Under never, the escalation path maps rejected to "the user rejected" even though no user was consulted packages/sandbox/sandbox/src/escalation.ts:199-205. The audit event is correct; the text blames a person.

The clearance desk below lets you choose a mode and action, then watch which layer refuses it, whether approval is asked, and what the log records

Interactive · 1

Who can say yes, and what can the process touch?

Combine approval policy, answerer availability, sandbox mode, and enforcement completeness. See which layer refuses and what it records.

Mechanism summary

Approval answers whether this specific action may proceed; only allowed-once is a grant, and an absent or failed answerer becomes unavailable. Sandboxing governs file effects of a spawned process, not network or process visibility. A backend can report partial enforcement, and a caller that needs an absolute boundary must not treat that as full.

Teaching model: the controls simplify real timing and concurrency; the rules follow the pinned source. Sources: approval outcomes   sandbox policy and enforcement

.

The execution world behind the policy

A path policy only means something inside one execution world. Both providers share a host filesystem and the policy root, so a path the fence allows names the same file the shell sees. A bash call's workdir can differ from the workspace root; the fence still checks the policy root. The policy service preserves the session cwd's spelling; the enforcing provider canonicalizes the root where the files exist, so a cwd containing symlink/.. resolves to the directory the paired subprocess provider runs in packages/sandbox/sandbox-policy/src/index.ts:35-39.

That agreement is a deployment property. A remote sandbox paired with a remote filesystem moves both and the policy together. A host filesystem paired with a remote shell breaks the assumption: the fence canonicalizes one world while the command runs in another.

What transfers

Copy the closed outcome. A boolean permission API has already lost the difference between "no", "withdrawn", and "nobody answered". Those need different model-facing text and operator responses. Only one value grants; make every other value deny.

Copy the placement of never inside the service, before the answerer chain. A listener gate inherits listener ordering, and ordering is not a security property. Copy the per-call policy: mode, root, and session identity travel to the enforcing boundary, so concurrent calls can use different boundaries without mutating provider state.

Copy enforcement honesty. Return full or partial with the result, and make the caller decide whether partial is acceptable. Fail closed when no backend exists. Do not let a missing runner become an unconfined run, and do not let a denied command become a generic exit code.

Do not copy the whole platform matrix for one platform and one trusted user. A single in-process fence can be proportionate when the model supplies paths but never code. Do not treat approval as a substitute for confinement: if an action is irreversible, the boundary must hold after the answer. Do not extend the vocabulary to network or process isolation by implication.

Back in the scenario, the edit is granted once, the test runs under the standing mode, and the audit log holds two records explaining why the wider call was allowed. The next edit asks again.

Part III · Trust and Time/Chapter 08

Survive the Crash, Keep the Story

Write handles, flush barriers, JSONL generations, repair, resume, and fork.

≈ 11 min read4 figures1 interactionSource 687f282e
In this chapter · 8 sections
  1. Two acknowledgements, one door
  2. From append to fsync
  3. What the crash leaves behind
  4. Who owns the write
  5. The header, the cut, and the generations
  6. Where the mechanisms live
  7. Failures and costs
  8. What transfers

The failing-test scenario reaches its first write at 14:07. The agent has read src/cart.test.ts and src/cart.ts, decided the tax change broke the discount total, and issued an edit tool call against src/cart.ts. The edit tool opens the file and writes the new calculation. Before it returns a result the loop can record, the process dies.

The next process finds a session log that ends with an open turn, a tool/call for the edit, and no tool/result for it. The log cannot say whether the edit reached the file. It can say which part of the conversation was recorded before the kill, and the next agent must continue from that recorded intent without pretending the call either failed or succeeded.

The example is a teaching scenario, not a report of a run; the wall clock and file contents are invented.

This chapter follows one accepted event from Session.append into storage and back out through resume. DeepSeek Harness (DSH) is the runtime that composes the loop, tools, and storage around a model, and this is the durability half of its ledger. The loop and the session define what the conversation is; this layer defines how much of it survives.

Two acknowledgements, one door

A session is an append-only log of typed events, each with a contiguous sequence number, seq. A turn is one model-loop execution; a step is one model call and the tool calls it requested. A tool call is the model's request to run a tool; a tool result is the recorded outcome.

The persistence layer exposes one abstract service, ctx.sessionPersistence, and one open channel per stored session, a handle. A write handle is the session's single mutator; a read handle observes without owning. append adds a contiguous batch, flush is the durability barrier, and close releases the handle and, for a write handle, its ownership.

Two acknowledgements matter:

  • A resolved append means the batch is accepted, ordered, and visible to later reads on the same backend instance. It does not promise crash survival; a backend may buffer or batch physical writes behind it.
  • A resolved flush means every acknowledged append is durable and the session is materialized for other processes.

The contract says this directly packages/session/session-persistence/src/handle.ts:85-109. In the shipped JSONL backend, an explicit append already writes and fsyncs its batch. The live path is different: the session publishes each event synchronously to session/event, and the backend copies it into a bounded write-behind window. The first buffered event starts a 200 ms deadline; later events join without extending it packages/session/session-persistence-jsonl/src/storage.ts:35-36. A crash can lose that window even though the session accepted every event in it.

A crash during a write can leave a torn record: bytes with no newline or a partial compression frame. A reader never serves it. It serves the valid prefix, the longest run of complete event records from seq 0, and the write path truncates the torn bytes before its first new append packages/session/session-persistence/src/index.ts:117-136.

From append to fsync

Four stages:

  1. Session.append snapshots the event data, validates it, pushes the frozen event into the in-memory log, and synchronously notifies session/event observers packages/core/session/src/index.ts:876-897.
  2. When the 200 ms timer fires or a flush arrives, drainBuffered splices the buffer into one batch and calls persistContiguous packages/session/session-persistence-jsonl/src/storage.ts:288-316.
  3. persistContiguous takes the write lease if needed, checks that the batch continues the stored next-seq, commits any pending torn-tail repair, then writes the batch packages/session/session-persistence-jsonl/src/storage.ts:318-343.
  4. For an existing JSONL artifact, appendLines encodes the batch as one Zstandard frame (or raw lines), appends it, and fsyncs. If the write or sync fails, it truncates back to the previous size before rethrowing, so a retry cannot create duplicate sequence numbers packages/session/session-persistence-jsonl/src/index.ts:1406-1439.

A session that has never materialized has no artifact. Its first write goes through materialize: encode the header line and first batch, write and fsync a temporary file, publish it with link so a concurrent creator cannot be overwritten, then fsync the directory so the new entry survives a power loss packages/session/session-persistence-jsonl/src/index.ts:1262-1322. Until then the session exists only in the creating process; one that never materializes before a crash never existed as stored history.

The loop does not flush at every turn boundary. A checkpoint policy owns the semantic barriers: before a model request is dispatched, before a top-level tool body runs, and before each step packages/session/session-checkpoint-policy/src/index.ts:52-82. That is why the edit call is durable before the edit executes: tool/call is appended, the checkpoint flushes, and only then does the tool body touch src/cart.ts packages/core/agent-loop/src/tool-calls.ts:166-174.

The barrier is fail-closed. If the flush rejects, the adapter is not called and the tool body is not run. A durability failure becomes a visible error before a side effect, not after it.

What the crash leaves behind

The durable tail looks like this:

Text
turn/start         durable
step/start         durable
assistant/message  durable
tool/call          durable
tool/result        (missing)
step/end           (missing)
turn/end           (missing)

Persistence returns the complete prefix up to the tool call. It does not append a synthetic result and it does not truncate the open turn. Truncating would discard durably recorded work; a long turn can contain many steps and large tool outputs. The storage layer repairs only the physical tail: it truncates a torn fragment and rewrites complete records recovered from a torn frame before the next append. Semantic repair belongs to the reader docs/subsystems/persistence.md:108-112.

Resume is that reader. It opens for write first, claiming in-process ownership and the cross-process lease before reading. It reads the valid prefix, computes closer events, appends them through the same handle as one batch, prepares an unpublished Session from the prefix plus the closers, and only then publishes the agent packages/core/agent-loop/src/index.ts:843-899.

The closer set has a fixed order. Missing tool results come first, in assistant order. Then one step/end if a step was open. Then one turn/end whose reason is { kind: 'interrupted' } packages/core/session/src/repair.ts:43-98. The excerpt shows the last two:

Text
Actual source, repair.ts:92-97
  // Close an open step before its turn.
  if (openStep !== null) {
    closers.push({ type: 'step/end', seq: SessionSeq(seq++), time, data: { turn: openTurn, step: openStep } })
  }
  closers.push({ type: 'turn/end', seq: SessionSeq(seq++), time, data: { turn: openTurn, reason: { kind: cause.kind } } })

interrupted is repair-only. The loop never emits it live; resume appends it for a log whose last turn never ended, and a read-only observer synthesizes it in memory. forked has the same status for a fork cut inside an open turn packages/core/session/src/types.ts:199-233. Keeping these reasons out of the live loop means a crash cannot look like a decision the loop made.

For the edit, the closer is a tool/result with isError: true, code TOOL_OUTCOME_UNKNOWN, and text saying the outcome is unknown, to retry only when the operation is read-only or idempotent, and not to retry blindly packages/core/session/src/repair.ts:31-35. The harness does not retry the edit. The next request derives history from the repaired log, so the error is model-visible, and the model can read src/cart.ts to learn whether the write landed.

A call with no recorded tool/call gets TOOL_NOT_STARTED; a started call has an unknown outcome.

The crash-point picker below lets you move the kill from request dispatch to the tool body and compare the recovered log, the repair batch, and the retry decision. Its learning question is which failures the durable log can actually distinguish, and which ones it can only report as unknown.

Interactive · 1

Which failures can the recovered log distinguish?

Move the crash from an unflushed prompt to an unanswered tool call. Compare the durable prefix, the repair batch, and the model-visible result.

Mechanism summary

An append can be accepted in memory before it is durable; flush is the barrier. Storage returns only a valid contiguous prefix and repairs a torn physical tail. Resume takes write ownership, adds missing tool results as unknown or not started, closes an open step and turn as interrupted, and only then publishes the agent. A tool that may have run cannot be retried blindly.

Teaching model: the controls simplify real timing and concurrency; the rules follow the pinned source. Sources: interrupted turn closers   append and flush semantics

Who owns the write

Two writers on one log can produce duplicate sequence numbers or interleaved batches that no reader can repair. DSH excludes that at two levels.

In process, the backend maps a session id to its active write handle. create registers the id before returning; a second create rejects with SessionAlreadyExistsError. open(id, 'write') claims the id and rejects with SessionAlreadyOwnedError while another write handle is active packages/session/session-persistence-jsonl/src/storage.ts:414-432. A read handle claims nothing, so the UI and session-query can read a live session packages/session/session-persistence-jsonl/src/index.ts:393-420.

Across processes, the JSONL backend holds a kernel lock in the session directory: a non-blocking flock(2) on session.lock on POSIX, a named kernel semaphore on Windows. The kernel releases it when the holder's descriptor or last handle closes, including on process death, so a crashed writer never blocks its successor. There is no expiry: expiring a wedged but live writer could let a second process append while the first resumes and tears the log. Readers never touch the lock packages/session/session-persistence-jsonl/src/lease.ts:1-29.

A created session takes the lease lazily, just before its first materializing write, because an unmaterialized session has no filesystem footprint to contend over packages/session/session-persistence-jsonl/src/lease.ts:20-22. An opened write handle already holds it. Release closes the descriptor; the POSIX lock file stays so later lockers keep a stable inode to verify packages/session/session-persistence-jsonl/src/lease.ts:118-134.

Resume therefore cannot race a live turn in another process. If the original process is alive, the open rejects as already owned. If it is dead, the kernel has already dropped the lock.

The header, the cut, and the generations

The event log is replayable and model-visible; the header is immutable metadata beside it: format version, session id, creation time, working directory, parent session, the isSeeded lineage bit, optional origin, delegationDepth, and agentPreset packages/core/session/src/types.ts:92-132. None is an event, and none reaches deriveMessages(). A later host uses the header to restore the workspace, recursion budget, and agent composition instead of guessing them.

The exact fork cut is not a header field; the header carries only the isSeeded lineage bit. The cut is a tagged event, session/end-seed with { inherited: true }, at the child's first owned sequence number. The JSONL header line's comment says the exact inherited cut lives on the last tagged end-seed event packages/session/session-persistence-jsonl/src/format.ts:79-82. Readers validate that the bit and the marker agree; a seeded header whose last inherited marker is at a different sequence is refused as malformed packages/session/session-format-v3-to-v4/src/validation.ts:73-77.

A fork is a copy plus a marker plus closers. buildForkSeed copies the inclusive source prefix, appends the inherited marker at boundary + 1, then appends fork-cause closers packages/core/session/src/fork.ts:21-29. SessionStore.fork sets inheritedEventCount to the copied source count, sets isSeeded: true and parentSession, and creates a new id packages/core/session/src/index.ts:1380-1398.

The physical log is one immutable file per format generation. Version 0 keeps session.jsonl; later generations add a lowercase numeric component, so version 4 is session.v4.jsonl, or session.v4.jsonl.zstd with compression packages/session/session-persistence-jsonl/src/format.ts:50-77. Only canonical names count: no temporary suffix, no uppercase, no leading zero, no .v0.

Opening selects the numerically highest canonical generation. A future generation refuses with an upgrade message even when an older readable one exists packages/session/session-persistence-jsonl/src/index.ts:596-614.

A read open decodes and migrates a historical generation into current logical values in memory, then returns a handle over that result without publishing. No source path, byte, or inode changes. A write open is stricter: it holds the claim and lease, reuses the prepared migration, publishes the current generation exclusively, and only then returns a writable handle packages/session/session-persistence-jsonl/src/index.ts:744-767. The old file stays beside it, unchanged.

Where the mechanisms live

Failures and costs

A crash inside the 200 ms window loses buffered events. A crash before the first checkpoint can lose the prompt batch and the opening turn/start; a later loss can include a tool/result that the tool already produced. The log cannot distinguish "the tool did not finish" from "the tool finished and the record was still buffered." Both become TOOL_OUTCOME_UNKNOWN, the honest answer and a real cost: the model must verify external state.

A crash between the last append of a turn and the next checkpoint can lose turn/end. Resume then closes a turn that actually completed and labels it interrupted. The repair is conservative about ordering, not clairvoyant about completion. The model sees a transcript that may claim less progress than the session made.

The 200 ms number bounds the wait before a write starts, not scheduling or device latency. A slow fsync extends the exposure, and no number is a durability guarantee.

A live but wedged writer keeps the lease until its process exits, so resume rejects with SessionAlreadyOwnedError rather than risk two writers; an operator must kill it. Read-only access still works, so the session stays inspectable.

Repair closes turn, step, and tool boundaries. It does not close plugin-owned brackets such as compaction/*; those belong to the plugin that opened them docs/subsystems/session.md:737-743. A plugin that needs stronger recovery has to define its own closers or tolerate an open bracket.

Immutable generations accumulate. A format upgrade writes a new file and keeps the old one, so disk use grows with the number of generations present, and the first write open after an upgrade pays a full decode and a verified rewrite. A future format refuses to open, so downgrading the harness does not read a newer log. That refusal is deliberate: guessing at a newer vocabulary could reconstruct a wrong conversation.

The header and the body share one consistency rule. The isSeeded bit lives in the header; the exact cut lives in the event log. A backend that stores the header but drops the marker, or the reverse, produces a refused log rather than a silently unseeded one.

What transfers

The shape is small. Separate acceptance from durability, and make the durable barrier explicit. Put all log access behind one owned handle and keep replayable events apart from metadata the model must never see. Store one immutable file per format generation and never rewrite a source. Do the semantic repair at the reader that owns the turn model, not in the storage backend. Take the write claim before reading so repair cannot race a live writer.

An explicit barrier means callers must know their real durability points; DSH puts them at model dispatch and top-level tool bodies, the smallest set that prevents an unrecorded side effect. A single-writer lease means a stuck process can block recovery. Conservative repair means the model sometimes has to verify work that already succeeded.

A smaller harness can drop some of this. If only one process can ever open a session, an in-process claim is enough and the kernel lock is overhead. If the store is a transactional database, the generation directory and the file lease disappear, and the append/flush split can collapse into one commit. What should not collapse is the separation between the physical prefix and the semantic turn: the storage layer can tell you which bytes are valid, and only the turn model can tell you what those bytes mean.

Back in the failing-test scenario, the next process opens the log, reads the durable prefix, appends an unknown-outcome result for the edit, closes the step and turn as interrupted, and publishes the agent. The next turn begins from repaired history. The model reads src/cart.ts before it edits again. The record now preserves both the work and the uncertainty about whether the edit landed.
