Part IV · Scale and Surface/Chapter 09

Children With Their Own Logs

Local and external subagents, ownership, cancellation, and continuation.

≈ 11 min read3 figures1 interactionSource 687f282e
In this chapter · 9 sections
  1. The seam above the loop
  2. Two kinds of child
  3. Activation, identity, and delivery
  4. The normal trace
  5. Ownership on two planes
  6. Continuation is a new activation
  7. Cancellation, depth, and cost
  8. Source map
  9. What carries forward

The discount test is failing, and its log is four thousand lines long. The parent agent has src/cart.ts open, a suspected double tax application, and no reason to pull the whole log into its own context. It asks a child to read the log and name the first assertion that diverges, then returns to the edit.

Delegation looks like a function call with a long return path. Four properties make it safe. The child needs an identity the parent can name later. The parent needs a way to stop it. The work needs to survive a restart. The result needs a route home that does not pretend the child's transcript was the parent's. Lose one and the delegation becomes an orphan process, a duplicate agent, a lost result, or a false completion.

This chapter follows one delegation from the tool call to the settlement notice. It sits above the agent loop: the loop executes a subagent tool, and the delegation seam owns what follows.

The seam above the loop

A seam is an interface with interchangeable providers and policy at the boundary. DSH uses it for models, tools, sandboxes, and persistence. Delegation adds a service, ctx.subagents, with a provider registry and consumer tools.

A provider knows how to make a child or how to talk to one. The manager knows who owns the child, whether the parent may start it, when it has finished, and what happens to its resources. A local provider implements prepareContinuable and returns creation data: whether the child Session starts with a prefix of the parent's log. An external provider implements start and returns a SubagentRun handle. Method presence selects the execution kind before the manager reserves anything.packages/subagent/subagent/src/index.ts:269-284

The manager owns identity, composition, delivery, resume, and teardown. A provider for a continuable child never sees its Agent, handle, turns, or teardown.packages/subagent/subagent/src/types.ts:340-355

Two kinds of child

A local child is a new Agent on the same Cordis context. It gets its own Session, system prompt, tool composition, and model route. The manager creates the Agent and keeps its AgentHandle. The spawn provider contributes nothing, so context does not transfer: the child starts fresh. The fork provider contributes a seed: every event up to and including the parent's last turn/end. The in-flight turn is excluded because it is unbalanced and cannot be replayed as a valid child session.packages/subagent/subagent-fork-in-process/src/index.ts:46-78

An external child is a runtime the provider starts elsewhere. It has no local Session. The DSH SDK provider launches a complete harness process with its own profile, patches, session, model route, and tools over stdio JSON-RPC. No Cordis context crosses, and the child starts fresh.packages/subagent/subagent-dsh-sdk/src/index.ts:119-166

A local child accepts later messages and can cold-resume from its own log. An external child is one execution. It rejects follow-up input, and a parent-delivery notice says so.packages/subagent/subagent/src/activation.ts:115-123

Activation, identity, and delivery

An activation is one managed execution period for one child. It is not the child: the Session outlives the activation, and a later message creates a new activation on the same Session.

The activation holds an AgentHandle or SubagentRun, a result promise, dispose(), a capacity slot, the parent edge, and a shared close transaction. dispose() addresses that exact activation, never a later resume of the same child id.packages/subagent/subagent/src/types.ts:46-59

A local child's identity is a SessionId that serves as the Session id, the Agent id, and the name the parent later passes to send_message. The header records the durable part: parent Session, subagent origin, fork seed flag, and delegation depth. It survives resume.packages/core/session/src/types.ts:105-124

The child's log carries a subagent/descriptor event with the provider, continuation mode, label, and the route or composition needed to resume. It is log-only: no surface operation, no model history, and it survives compaction.packages/subagent/subagent/src/descriptor.ts:29-48 Policy events record the sandbox mode, approval policy, and permission preset captured at delegation, so the child's scope is reconstructable from its log.packages/subagent/subagent/src/child-agent.ts:248-279

The parent writes a catalog event, subagent/catalog, once per local child. It records membership, not status: an id, creation time, mode, and label.packages/subagent/subagent/src/catalog.ts:139-151

delivery: 'parent' sends the model a settlement notice and is what the subagent tool uses. delivery: 'caller' returns the result to the awaiting program and emits no notice; the workflow host uses this form.packages/workflow/workflow-ptc/src/host.ts:203-220

Delegation depth is the recursion budget: zero at top level, one for its child. The value is stored in the child header, and the runtime reads the larger of the stored value and its runtime option, so a resumed child cannot delegate as if it were top-level.packages/subagent/subagent/src/depth.ts:28-36

The normal trace

The subagent call carries a description, prompt, and optional directory. For the triage, the prompt is the log path, the question, and the no-edit instruction. The tool resolves the child route and depth, then calls startActivation with parent delivery and the tool call's cancellation signal.packages/subagent/tool-subagent/src/index.ts:330-337

The manager runs this sequence.packages/subagent/subagent/src/manager.ts:379-405

  1. Check admission, require persistence for parent delivery, and reserve a child id. Compute childDepth = parentDepth + 1 and reject it above the cap.
  2. Snapshot descriptor and policy before the first await, resolve the directory, and ask the provider for creation input: none for spawn, the completed-turn prefix for fork.
  3. Under a per-child lock, reserve capacity, create the Agent, append descriptor and policy, register the activation, add the child to the parent's owned set, and emit subagent/start.

The header records the creation fields.packages/subagent/subagent/src/child-agent.ts:135-154

Text
Actual source, child-agent.ts:143-153
  return {
    ...parentHeader.cwd !== undefined ? { cwd: parentHeader.cwd } : {},
    ...agentPreset === undefined ? {} : { agentPreset },
    parentSession: parentHeader.id,
    isSeeded,
    // Navigation classification only; the descriptor remains the authority
    // for mode and continuation capability.
    origin: 'subagent',
    // Durable: the recursion budget must survive persistence and resume.
    delegationDepth: childDepth,
  }

The prompt goes to the child's inbox, the catalog fact is appended to the parent Session, and startActivation resolves with the child id and message id.packages/subagent/subagent/src/manager.ts:459-471 The tool returns started subagent <id>. The parent does not wait; the tool result excludes output.

Acceptance is precise: the test asserts that the id is returned before the child logs its prompt or requests a model.packages/subagent/subagent/tests/continuation.spec.ts:509-529 If acceptance fails, the activation is disposed and the child rolled back.

Teaching pseudocode for the local path, with locking and rollback folded away:

Text
Teaching pseudocode: startLocalChild
  childId = reserved or new SessionId
  depth = parent.depth + 1; assert depth <= maxDepth
  seed = provider.prepareSeed(parent)   # local only
  slot = pool.reserve(capacity)
  handle = agents.create(childId, {
    parentSession: parent.id, origin: 'subagent',
    isSeeded: seed present, delegationDepth: depth })
  append(descriptor, policy)
  resident[childId] = Activation(handle, slot, parent)
  parent.ownedChildren.add(childId)
  accept(initial prompt); append(parent, catalog, childId)
  return { childId, messageId }

The child then works in its own Session. The manager waits for three conditions: idle child, no unclaimed inbox input, no unfinished children. Then it flushes, captures the result, closes the activation, disposes the handle, releases the slot, and sends the notice.packages/subagent/subagent/src/manager.ts:1023-1090

The result comes from the child's own log: the last non-empty assistant message, or the accumulated assistant text stream, or an empty output.packages/subagent/subagent/src/assistant-output.ts:50-59 The stop reason also comes from the log, not from the fact that teardown succeeded. A clean disposal does not turn a failed child into a completed one.packages/subagent/subagent/src/lifecycle.ts:119-134

For parent delivery, the manager builds a user-role notice attributed to subagent-settled, separate from an agent-authored message. It names the child, states how it ended, carries the closing text, and appends structured output or a diagnostic.packages/subagent/subagent/src/continuation-messages.ts:138-167 A busy parent gets it at its next step; an idle parent starts a turn.packages/subagent/subagent/src/manager.ts:1187-1206

Ownership on two planes

Ownership runs on two planes that fail differently.

The durable plane is the catalog and the child header: the parent Session holds the catalog fact, the child Session holds parentSession and the subagent origin. listChildren reads the catalog projection without opening the child log or resuming an Agent.packages/subagent/subagent/src/list-children.ts:31-53 Membership survives the activation and can be read later.

The live plane is the manager's resident map and each activation's ownedChildren set. A parent activation with an unfinished child cannot settle; the child id stays in the set until disposal releases it. Disposing a parent cancels it, disposes owned children before the parent handle, and flushes after idle.packages/subagent/subagent/src/manager.ts:1094-1124 The close transaction is shared and idempotent, so natural settlement, explicit dispose, and host drain converge on one teardown.packages/subagent/subagent/src/manager.ts:770-781

The catalog records belonging; the resident map records handles. A restart keeps the first and loses the second, so cold resume needs both a persisted child Session and a live parent Agent.

The delegation tree below lets you spawn a child, cancel the parent, and resume; its learning question is which ownership edges survive each action.

Interactive · 1

What survives when a child is cancelled?

Spawn a local child, settle it, cancel it, or dispose the parent. Track the child session, activation ownership, cancellation, and result delivery.

Mechanism summary

A child has its own session and scope. The manager owns the live activation and capacity slot; the parent session owns durable catalog membership. Cancelling or disposing an activation stops child work, but persisted membership and the child session can remain. Parent disposal alone does not stop live children; a host that owns the manager must drain descendants or dispose the activation. A continuable child resumes through a new activation under the same id; an external execution does not.

Teaching model: the controls simplify real timing and concurrency; the rules follow the pinned source. Sources: activation and delivery   local child sequence

Continuation is a new activation

After the child settles, its activation is gone but its Session remains. A later send_message to the child id enters coldResume: observe the persisted Session, check that its header names the sending parent, fold the first supported descriptor, rebuild the route and composition, materialize a new activation, and submit the message.packages/subagent/subagent/src/manager.ts:1329-1376 No subagent provider is dispatched; the descriptor supplies every reconstruction input.packages/subagent/subagent/src/manager.ts:1325-1328

Continuation is therefore not another prompt in the parent session. The new turn lands in the child's own log under the same id and composition. The parent gets a new notice, not the child's transcript. The child stays addressable because id and descriptor persist, not because the parent kept a handle. There is no durable parent mailbox: a child's message to a parent that is not live is rejected.

Only a direct child can be cold-resumed. The parent must be the exact live Agent in the header, and the child must carry a current continuable descriptor. A missing or unsupported descriptor returns NOT_RESUMABLE rather than falling back to the parent's composition.

sendMessage requires the exact live sender. A sender may target a direct continuable child. A resident continuable child may target its direct parent. A sibling is neither, so it cannot address the other child.packages/subagent/subagent/src/manager.ts:543-574 Interrupt authority is also lineage-based: a sibling or unrelated agent is rejected, and a self-interrupt is rejected.packages/subagent/tool-subagent-control/tests/tool-subagent-control.spec.ts:468-506

The initial task may tell the child to send a self-contained result to the parent id, because the parent shares the workspace but not the transcript, tool output, or reasoning.packages/subagent/subagent/src/continuation-messages.ts:80-96

Cancellation, depth, and cost

Cancellation authority changes once. Before inbox acceptance, the tool call's signal is the channel: aborting it rolls back an unaccepted child and leaves no resident activation or catalog fact. After acceptance, the manager owns the activation. Coverage asserts that aborting the caller signal after acceptance leaves the turn running.packages/subagent/subagent/tests/continuation.spec.ts:3472-3490 Before the receipt the caller has nothing to dispose; after it the signal stops.

The model's stop path is interrupt_agent. For a local child, the manager cancels the current turn with cause parent or user and keeps the inbox. Unclaimed follow-ups are parked. The activation stays resident while the inbox holds input, and a later waking send_message can resume the queue.packages/subagent/subagent/src/manager.ts:220-227packages/subagent/subagent/src/manager.ts:1087-1090 Interrupt is not disposal: if nothing wakes the parked child, disposal or a drain ends it.

dispose closes admission, cancels when asked, disposes owned children first, waits for idle, flushes, releases the handle and slot, sends any parent notice, and resolves the result. Teardown failure rejects dispose and marks the lifecycle end failed, but does not replace a captured result.packages/subagent/subagent/src/manager.ts:1175-1183 External children have a shorter path: interrupt aborts the controller and disposes the handle; no inbox, no later resume.

Depth is enforced at start, not by hiding the tool. The default is one, so a top-level agent may create direct children and a depth-one child may not create grandchildren.packages/subagent/subagent/src/index.ts:195-198 The child still sees the tool, and its runtime context says zero levels remain; the runtime rejects a start that ignores it.packages/subagent/tool-subagent/src/index.ts:382-394

Capacity is separate: a top-level parent starts a pool of eight shared by its descendants; the root consumes no slot.packages/subagent/subagent/src/index.ts:197 Reservation precedes creation; the slot returns after cleanup. At capacity, creation rejects instead of queueing.

The shared checkout is the cost delegation does not solve. The child gets a directory, not a copy, defaulting to the parent's effective directory. There is no branch, merge, or conflict check. Telling the child not to edit files is a prompt instruction, not a filesystem boundary. The parent owns integration: it must avoid concurrent writes and inspect what changed. The child's scope is captured at delegation with approval pinned to never when approval is composed; it cannot ask for wider access, though it can write anywhere its inherited sandbox allows.

Local parent delivery requires persistence, and cold resume requires session query.packages/subagent/subagent/src/manager.ts:383packages/subagent/subagent/src/manager.ts:1471-1479 The final flush is best effort: a failure is logged and the child may be stale on resume.packages/subagent/subagent/src/manager.ts:1208-1218 A host that never drains can leave live activations after the parent leaves; parent disposal does not stop them.packages/subagent/subagent/src/manager.ts:235-245

Teaching model. The storefront repository, the 4,000-line log, and the child's triage are invented to make the delegation concrete. Event types, header fields, ownership rules, and failure paths come from the pinned source. The pseudocode folds locking, capacity, and rollback into single steps.

What carries forward

Delegation is safe when four things have one owner each. Identity belongs to the durable Session. Lifetime belongs to the manager and its activation. Delivery belongs to explicit policy. Cancellation belongs to a receipt that marks where the caller's signal stops and the manager's ownership begins.

A smaller harness can copy this: give every child a durable id and a parent link. Keep a live registry of activations separate from durable membership. Let the provider contribute data or a handle, and let one component own creation, settlement, and disposal. Persist depth and resume configuration in the child's record, so a restart can distinguish a child that never existed from one whose activation ended.

Do not copy this shape for a one-shot call with no follow-up and no parent-facing notice; use caller delivery and let the caller own the result. Do not use it to isolate two agents editing the same files. The checkout is shared, and the parent owns the merge.

For the failing test, the division is modest. The child reads the log and reports the first divergence. The parent keeps the checkout and decides what to change. The child can be asked again because it has its own log, and stopped because the current activation has an owner.

Part IV · Scale and Surface/Chapter 10

The Browser Is Another Plugin Tree

Host authority, remotes, follow baselines, conversation targets, and reconnect.

≈ 11 min read4 figures1 interactionSource 687f282e
In this chapter · 9 sections
  1. The boundary and its terms
  2. Boot: composition arrives as data
  3. Remotes are functions, not shared objects
  4. Following a durable journal
  5. From one window to two views
  6. The drop
  7. Why there is no universal resync
  8. What transfers
  9. Source map

The discount test is failing again. The developer has already sent the prompt from the browser: find the cause, fix src/cart.ts, run pnpm vitest run src/cart.test.ts. The transcript shows the read of src/cart.test.ts, the edit to the total calculation, and a test row that is still running. Then the network drops.

Three responses are available. Reload the page, and lose the scroll position, the draft, and the local echo of a prompt that may already be durable. Keep the rendered DOM and pretend it is current, even though the test result may have arrived after the disconnect. Or treat the page as a client of the Host's log, with explicit rules for what is replaced, what is retained, and what is lost.

DSH takes the third. The browser runs its own Cordis plugin tree, but it owns no durable state. Host controllers own the session (the durable log of one conversation), the mutation order, and the streams. Every browser view derives from explicit inputs with a stated recovery rule, and the connection is replaceable rather than the source of truth.

This chapter follows one session out of the Host and into the browser. It uses the log from Chapter 4 and the boot composition from Chapter 2.

Teaching model. The failing-test transcript is the book's running example; its details are illustrative. The protocol behavior below is source-backed.

The boundary and its terms

A Host is the Node process that owns sessions, files, policy, and mutation ordering. Host authority covers durable state, persistence and mutation order, access policy, and stream production.docs/subsystems/web-client.md:11-20 A client can cache, merge, and display. It cannot adjudicate.

A client is the browser-side Cordis application. It has its own context, services, effects, and disposal path. It is replaceable because its contract is a set of remotes: generated methods and streams whose argument and result shapes are fixed at build time. A Host object never crosses the wire. An Agent parameter becomes an agentId, and the Host resolves the id back to its object before the method runs.docs/api-gateway.md:11

A client model is a React-free object that mirrors one Host domain. It owns object identity, resolves races between unary responses and stream frames, and exposes observable snapshots plus commands. A projection is a derived view with explicit inputs; in the browser, every view snapshot is one.

A follow stream opens with a baseline: an opening snapshot at a cursor containing the header, complete projections, and a bounded tail page of durable records. It then carries increments in cursor order. The cursor is the inclusive position of the last applied durable record. A generation is one physical opening of a logical stream. Reconnecting opens a new generation; it does not continue the old one. A Connection generation is one established Host connection.

A conversation target is a named projection of the session event window with its own incremental builder and final snapshot. A slot is a typed React seat declared by its owner, with a cardinality and a scope.

Boot: composition arrives as data

The browser plugin graph is composed on the Host. ClientModuleRegistry scans the Loader's entries for packages whose manifest declares dsh.client with platform: 'web', reads their ./client export, and composes a WebBootGraph.packages/client/modules/src/index.ts:857-875 The graph holds entry rows in module-graph order and batches split into bootstrap and application phases.packages/client/modules/src/index.ts:774-790

The Host turns the graph into head rows: an inline queue-mode __ModuleLoader__ facade, preloads for application batches, blocking scripts for bootstrap batches, and the graph itself as globalThis["__DSH_BOOT__"].packages/client/modules/src/index.ts:548-594 The facade must exist before any bundle executes; the graph before the shell reads it.

In the browser, AppWebEntry.run waits for the bootstrap to settle, creates the module system from the graph, prefetches rows marked immediately, creates a Cordis Loader over that module system, and creates one entry per row.packages/client/web/src/boot.ts:56-91 bootClient then waits for quiescence and audits every entry.packages/client/web/src/boot-client.ts:36-56

The module system is a lazy CommonJS table. Executing a bundle only registers a factory under window.__ModuleLoader__.load. The factory runs on first require, and every module-body effect, including CSS injection, happens then.packages/client/modules/src/client/manifest.ts:9-24 Materialization is memoized, and a require cycle is fatal because factory-form CommonJS cannot hand out partial exports.packages/client/modules/src/client/system.ts:297-322

Two orders coexist, and confusing them leads to wrong predictions. Module-graph order decides only that a factory arrives before a consumer materializes it. Cordis service injection decides when a plugin activates. ClientEntries.start creates every row concurrently and then awaits the Loader.packages/client/modules/src/client/entries.ts:84-99 assertEntriesActive rejects the boot if any entry failed to import, failed to apply, or still waits for a missing service, and names each reason.packages/client/web/src/boot-client.ts:59-88

A malformed dsh.client declaration aggregates into one error listing every broken package, and a half-composed shell would render controls whose services do not exist.docs/subsystems/client-modules.md:96

The renderer is one plugin among them, marked immediately.packages/client/ui-renderer/package.json:29-33 It hydrates the framework-free boot page and calls renderSlot('root'), the only context-level slot render in the application.packages/client/ui-renderer/src/client/app.tsx:19-21packages/client/ui-renderer/src/client/index.ts:59-83

Release identity travels with the graph. A page applies a graph or rebuilt bundle only while the Host serves its boot release; another release waits for a reload.docs/subsystems/client-modules.md:90packages/client/modules/src/client/entries.ts:109-116

Remotes are functions, not shared objects

A Host service marks callable methods with @Remote or @RemoteScope. The build emits strict descriptors, runtime codecs, declaration merges, and source maps.docs/api-gateway.md:108-116 The client assembly mounts those contributions as a traced Cordis child service under ctx.remote.<namespace>, and each method is a concrete function. No JavaScript Proxy participates in lookup or invocation.docs/api-gateway.md:62

The same wire lets a desktop shell, a worker preview, or a test carrier supply different ClientTransportHooks for fetching, stream opening, and bundle loading while the generated namespaces stay identical.packages/client/connection/src/client/index.ts:84-114

Streams use the same Connection generation. A method marked mode: 'stream' returns an async iterable on the Host and a stream handle on the client. The Gateway owns transport dispatch, cancellation, and stream supervision.docs/api-gateway.md:60 Every endpoint is access-controlled: session.follow and session.page declare a session resource reader, so a non-owner caller is admitted only by a policy role that covers that session.packages/api/session-controller/README.md:36

Following a durable journal

The session client is layered. ClientSessions owns references and stable bindings, SessionManager owns the list baseline and lazy instances, and each Session owns one contiguous window of SessionEventLikeEntry values: either a durable event or a client-only assistant/live-chunk presentation.docs/subsystems/web-client.md:42-48 Opening the Session calls follow(), and the Host's first frame is the opening snapshot: header, cursor, a bounded tail page of records, hasMore, projections at the cursor, and an Assistant stream baseline.packages/api/session-controller/src/history.ts:179-203

After the snapshot, the Host yields durable events only when the sequence is exactly the next expected value. A skipped sequence is a protocol error, not something the client should paper over.packages/api/session-controller/src/history.ts:213-233

RemoteJournalStream owns the client side of that contract. It validates every page and entry by inclusive cursor range. A replacement page must be contiguous and must end exactly at the cursor it was requested through. An entry that partially overlaps the last applied range is a violation; a fully older entry is ignored.packages/api/gateway/src/client/journal-stream.ts:305-336

Text
Actual source, journal-stream.ts:83-88
 * Owns snapshot-first opening, ordered live delivery, pagination, and repair.
 *
 * The domain retains its published window during reconnection. A replacement is
 * published only after the opening page reaches the generation's cursor.
 * Notifications never change a cursor and wait behind an in-flight gap repair.

The stream publishes three changes. The first frame of a generation becomes replace. A contiguous tail becomes append. An older page becomes prepend. A gap does not become a series of synthetic patches: the stream reads a page through the missing cursor and publishes the result as replace.packages/api/gateway/src/client/journal-stream.ts:338-395

Teaching pseudocode for the reconciliation rule, with cancellation and notifications omitted:

Text
on generation_opened(opening):
    assert opening.page.tail == opening.cursor
    publish replace(opening.page)

on entry(entry):
    if entry.last <= last_cursor: return
    if entry.first != last_cursor + 1:
        page = read_page(through=entry.last)
        publish replace(page)
        return
    last_cursor = entry.last
    publish append(entry)

On reconnect, the old window stays published while the carrier retries. A resumed cursor behind the last applied entry is a protocol violation rather than a silent rewind.packages/api/gateway/src/client/journal-stream.ts:269-302

The conversation layer sees a revision and an exact delta. It accepts only revision plus one with a non-replace change; a jump rebuilds the whole window.packages/client/ui-conversation/src/client/conversation/assembly.ts:107-139

Assistant text needs one more rule because tokens are not durable records. The Host's accumulator keeps a compact stream for the active attempt, and the follow baseline carries it. On replace, the client expands that stream into synthetic assistant/live-chunk entries whose fractional sequence positions place them between durable records. The in-progress answer reappears where it was, without durable token rows.packages/api/session-controller/src/client/sessions/assistant-stream.ts:58-101 If an index gap appears, the fold returns rebaseline and the Session reopens follow once for a paired page and baseline.packages/api/session-controller/src/client/sessions/session.ts:707-714

Control and workspace data have a different shape. They are materialized Host state, so every generation opens with a complete baseline and then applies increments. RemoteSnapshotStream enforces exactly one opening snapshot per generation and rejects any delta that arrives before it.packages/api/gateway/src/client/snapshot-stream.ts:67-89 The Workspace stream applies upsert, remove, order, archived, and pinned increments on top of that baseline.packages/api/workspace-controller/src/client/index.ts:78-96

Ordinary forwarded notifications are the third shape. A forwarded event is delivered once through ctx.remote.$on; it has no cursor, and the protocol carries no replay log.packages/api/gateway/src/client/remote-events.ts:115-120 Reconnect therefore refreshes the list and projections instead of trusting a notification stream.

From one window to two views

The window feeds an assembler, not a component. ConversationNodeAssembler keeps Contexts keyed by (kind, id). Each registered Event Definition matches an event, folds deterministic state, and optionally materializes one node for one target. Locations are derived from durable turn and step boundaries, so a live append can file a node without scanning the window.packages/client/ui-conversation/src/client/conversation/assembler.ts:220-247

replaceWindow clears the Contexts and replays the complete window. flush then walks only the active targets; an inactive target does no work.packages/client/ui-conversation/src/client/conversation/assembler.ts:363-404 Activation is monotonic: the first activation builds the target and calls replace() once, and later live events call apply().packages/client/ui-conversation/src/client/conversation/assembler.ts:406-421

Chat and Trajectory are separate targets with separate builders. They may match the same event family, but neither imports the other's final display model.packages/client/ui-chat/src/client/conversation-nodes/chat-snapshot-builder.ts:1231-1236packages/client/ui-trajectory/src/client/trajectory-snapshot-builder.ts:303-311 In the failing-test session, the turn and step boundaries give the assembler its Locations. The read, edit, and test calls become Chat tool rows under the prompt and Trajectory records under the request header; neither view reads the other's snapshot.

The shell chooses a persisted view if it resolves, otherwise Chat.packages/client/ui-conversation/src/client/view-selection.ts:15-21 It then renders conversation.view filtered to that id, and the slot is a session-scoped list.packages/client/ui-conversation/src/client/skeleton/DefaultConversationViews.tsx:33-41 Chat's node slot is keyed by node kind, so one renderer can be replaced without touching the flow.packages/client/ui-chat/src/client/contract/slots.ts:397-409

Slots carry the composition contract. The owner declares the key in SlotMap, its cardinality and scope, and the props it passes. Registering into an undeclared slot throws.packages/client/ui-slots/src/index.ts:1207-1211 A feature contributes through ctx.slots.inject, which installs one effect per declaration lifetime, so unloading the plugin removes it.packages/client/ui-renderer/src/client/registry.ts:195-242 root is the only slot rendered through the Cordis service itself; every other slot renders through an authorized child renderer.docs/subsystems/slots.md:19

SessionProvider is how one page shows two sessions at once. A session-scoped slot inherits the surrounding binding unless the parent passes an explicit reference, in which case only that subtree is overridden.packages/client/ui-renderer/src/client/scoped-slots.tsx:512-526

The drop

  1. The carrier (the physical transport beneath the logical stream) fails. The Gateway classifies it as a carrier error, not a business error. RemoteStream keeps the logical stream alive and waits for a usable Connection generation; the Connection loop owns the backoff. A terminal error bypasses retry.packages/api/gateway/src/client/remote-stream.ts:129-142
  2. The old window stays published. No partial replacement is visible while the page is disconnected.packages/api/gateway/src/client/journal-stream.ts:214-217
  3. A new Connection generation is published, and API Gateway emits connection/reset.packages/api/gateway/src/client/index.ts:178-183
  4. The Session controller repairs its cached state. It clears projection stores, aborts in-flight projection reads, and refreshes the list and projections; the same generation subscriber restarts the control stream. This repair runs from the generation subscription, so it also covers a ready baseline that arrives before connection/reset.packages/api/session-controller/src/client/sessions/manager.ts:755-775packages/api/session-controller/src/client/index.ts:128-140
  5. Each open Session journal reopens follow. The new opening snapshot becomes replace; the assembler clears and replays; each active target rebuilds once.packages/client/ui-conversation/src/client/conversation/assembler.ts:226-247 The snapshot is a bounded tail page, so a long gap can shrink the loaded window; older rows return through paging.
  6. Optimistic echoes reconcile against the new baseline. A receipt-backed echo covered by the projections watermark retires as observed; an unconfirmed echo stays pending.packages/api/session-controller/src/client/sessions/session.ts:688-696

Forwarded notifications delivered during the gap are not replayed. Transient Assistant rows are reconstructed only for the attempt the baseline describes; a settled attempt comes back from its durable settlement. Drafts and scroll positions live in client-only stores; a stream replacement keeps them, a page reload does not.

The reconnect lab below drops the stream and restores it. Its learning question: which parts of the view are replaced from the Host baseline, which are retained by a client model, and which are lost?

Interactive · 1

What is replaced and what is lost on reconnect?

Cut the carrier, emit durable events and live chunks, then reconnect. Compare the host journal, the retained client window, and the new baseline.

Mechanism summary

A reconnect opens a new connection generation and a fresh opening frame for each logical stream. The durable journal replaces its retained window from an opening snapshot with a bounded tail and validates sequence ranges; older history returns through paging. Control and workspace streams replace from complete snapshots. Ordinary notifications and live chunks are not replayed.

Teaching model: the controls simplify real timing and concurrency; the rules follow the pinned source. Sources: reconnection rules   client layers

Why there is no universal resync

Three data shapes need three contracts. A durable journal has a total order and inclusive ranges, so it can validate a window and replace it exactly. Materialized control state has a complete current value, so it can replace wholesale but cannot replay deltas it did not retain. A forwarded notification has no position at all, so it can only be delivered once or re-queried.

One resync() would have to pick one of those shapes and impose it on the others. Replaying notifications would require a per-client notification log that the Host does not keep. Snapshotting every journal on every notification would turn a linear follow into repeated full reads. Persisting every projection as an event would duplicate the log.

DSH exposes the Connection generation as the one shared signal and lets each model own its recovery. The cost is visible: no instant guarantees that the transcript, the sidebar, and the projection values describe the same Host instant. Each domain is internally consistent, and the UI tolerates mixed vintages. A new client model must also implement and defend its own replacement rule; the Gateway supplies generation numbers and range checks, not domain semantics.

What transfers

Copy the shape: one authoritative writer per fact, a typed wire instead of shared objects, a baseline-plus-increment contract with explicit range validation, React-free client models that own merge rules, and a projection registry so a new view is additive.

Skip the machinery when the system is small. One bundle does not need a lazy CommonJS table. One view does not need a target registry. A page that holds nothing worth preserving can reload instead of resuming; that is a valid strategy.

Part IV · Scale and Surface/Chapter 11

What the Seams Buy You

Extension recipes, alternative designs, limits, and the transferable core.

≈ 11 min read4 figures1 interactionSource 687f282e
In this chapter · 8 sections
  1. The seam, without the slogan
  2. Reversibility is an execution property
  3. Three questions for a new behavior
  4. What the alternatives cost
  5. Where the design strains
  6. The failing test, one more time
  7. What carries forward
  8. Source map

The failing-test request has been followed from process launch to browser repaint. Along the way, one pattern repeats. A part of the system is isolated behind a contract, a concrete implementation is mounted beside it, and policy attaches at an event or service boundary. The loop stays narrow while models, tools, logs, policies, and surfaces change around it.

That pattern is easy to describe and hard to keep. This chapter asks what transfers. It separates design choices forced by the problem from choices that belong to DeepSeek Harness at its current scale. It also names where the choices stop paying.

The seam, without the slogan

A seam has three roles:

  • a service definition that declares an interface;
  • a provider that implements it;
  • a consumer that uses the interface.

docs/architecture.md:130-136

The roles can live in separate packages or in one, but all three have to exist. A provider without a consumer is dead code. A consumer that imports a concrete provider is a sealed dependency. A definition used by only one implementation and never substituted may still be a good unit of code, but it is not yet a seam.

DeepSeek Harness uses seams for model streaming, tools, session persistence, filesystem access, subprocesses, sandboxing, approval, compaction, subagents, and Web transport. The variety matters. Some seams are about a vendor. Some are about an execution world. Some are about a human decision. Some are about a product surface.

The filesystem and subprocess seams show why the triad is worth the ceremony. ctx.fs and ctx.subprocess are separate contracts, but they describe one execution world. Point both at a remote provider and Bash, file edits, and language-server work move together. Point one at a remote world and the other at the local machine, and the agent is editing one checkout while running tests in another. The seam does not prevent that mistake. It makes the pairing visible.

docs/architecture.md:130-136

The tool seam is different. It is not mainly a provider swap. It is the boundary between a model's request and an effect. The model sees a schema; the registry resolves a definition in the calling agent's scope; the pipeline lets policy decide; the body runs; the result is normalized. The seam supports many tools without making every tool implement approval, concurrency, or persistence.

A useful question for any proposed abstraction is: what role is missing? If the answer is "we have a definition and a consumer but only one provider, and we import it directly," the abstraction is unfinished. If the answer is "we have three providers and a consumer that keeps switching on their concrete types," the interface is too thin. The missing role tells you where to work.

Reversibility is an execution property

The plugin tree is often described as "everything is a plugin." The more precise claim is that contributions have a lifetime. A tool registration, prompt section, model adapter, event listener, or policy guard is an effect. Disposing the owning scope removes it.

That property is what makes hot reload, per-agent capability sets, and clean teardown possible. The tool registry returns a disposer from register(). A scoped registration made through an agent context disappears when that agent's scope unwinds. A provider registered for a subagent does not leak into the parent.

packages/core/tools/src/index.ts:1065-1096

Reversibility is not free. The system needs a scope for every registration, a disposal order, and a rule for what happens when disposal fails. It needs to distinguish a service that is absent from a service that is still activating. During boot, "present in config" and "running" are different states. During an agent's life, "registered" and "visible to this agent" are different questions.

The implementation also pays for persistence of identity. An agent's scope is more than a bag of overrides: it is a set of registrations whose ownership must outlive individual calls and end exactly once. The session's event vocabulary and the child catalog encode durable ownership; the live agent registry and scope encode ownership inside one process. A restart has to make those two planes agree.

This is the point where a smaller project should hesitate. If it has one process, one configuration, and no per-session variations, a static module registry is easier to reason about than a scoped effect system. The reversible tree pays when changes happen while the system is running, or when two agents in one process must see different capabilities.

Three questions for a new behavior

Most extension decisions can start with three questions. The answers point to a boundary before they point to a file.

Must the fact survive a restart? If it affects model context, replay, audit, or fork, it belongs in the session log. If it is a live notification, it belongs in an event or a stream. If it is a cache, it should be reconstructable and disposable. Writing model-visible state to an unlogged side channel breaks resume in a way that is hard to detect until the process restarts.

docs/architecture.md:118-126

Is this an action or a policy over an action? A new capability usually belongs in a tool: a definition, an output renderer, and an execute body. A rule about when tools may run belongs in tools/pre-execute, a guard, the approval seam, or the sandbox. Putting policy inside every tool duplicates it and makes the rules invisible to the rest of the deployment. Tools should describe what they do; the pipeline should decide whether they may.

Is this shared by every agent or scoped to one? A global provider changes the composition. A scoped registration changes one agent's world. The distinction matters for both visibility and teardown. A parent's restriction can mask an inherited tool, while a child's own registration stays visible to the child. The scope chain is the mechanism; the policy is the design.

The extension map below turns these questions into a lookup. It asks what you want to add, then shows the definition, provider, consumer, and the most common mistake.

Interactive · 1

Where should a new behavior attach?

Choose an extension goal and compare the seam, the roles you need to fill, the tests that protect it, and the common overreach.

Mechanism summary

Add a model provider at the LLM seam, a model-facing capability in the tool registry, policy in the tool waterfalls or approval seam, and a new execution world by swapping filesystem and subprocess together. A new browser view is a client target and slot. Only a different turn and step protocol should replace the loop factory.

Teaching model: the controls simplify real timing and concurrency; the rules follow the pinned source. Sources: where new behavior goes   reversible registration

A fourth question is easy to forget: who owns the failure? A model provider that times out fails a request. A tool body that throws produces a result. A missing sandbox backend fails closed. A browser with a broken stream can still display its retained window. The owner of a failure is part of the interface, not an implementation detail.

What the alternatives cost

None of these bets is the only reasonable design. A different starting point changes which problems are cheap.

A monolith with configuration flags. This is easier to read, debug, and deploy for one product. A single process with a fixed loop and a map of tools can ship a coding agent. It becomes expensive when several surfaces need different capabilities, when a provider is replaced per deployment, or when a plugin must be installed without forking the application. DSH chooses composition because it ships several products from one launcher. A one-product team may not need that.

An actor or workflow runtime. Actors give each agent a mailbox and a supervisor, and workflows give every step a durable definition. These models are strong when the graph is known in advance or the system spans many machines. DSH keeps a single-process loop with an event log and adds subagent providers for delegation. That is simpler for interactive coding, where the model decides the next step at runtime. It is weaker for long-running distributed workflows with many independent tasks.

A database as the source of truth. A relational store can provide transactions, queries, and migration tooling. DSH uses an append-only event log and immutable JSONL generations. The log is better for exact replay and model reconstruction; a database is better for ad hoc joins and concurrent reporting. The choice is not about which storage is more modern. It is about which facts need to be reconstructed byte-for-byte and which need to be queried flexibly.

A universal event bus. A bus would make every subsystem look alike. DSH instead distinguishes session events, live agent events, capability events, and process-local notifications. That is more types to learn. It also prevents a UI chunk from being mistaken for durable history, or a policy veto from being replayed as a model message. Uniformity is not free when the audiences differ.

The trade-off table is a design ledger, not a scorecard. A small project should copy the part of the ledger that matches its actual pressure. It should not copy a layer because the source repository has one.

Where the design strains

Several costs recur across chapters.

A plugin boundary is not a security boundary

Plugins run in the same Node process and can reach the same resources. The launcher checks package compatibility and activation, not intent. Approval and sandboxing are separate mechanisms with their own limits. The source says compatibility checks are not a sandbox against malicious package code. A deployment that installs untrusted plugins needs process or container isolation outside this tree.

Configuration is code

A profile patch can contain !!js expressions evaluated against a plugin context. --dump-config composes the tree without importing modules or evaluating those expressions. --dump-config-schema imports each composed module to read its schema, so it executes trusted package code. A review of the YAML is partly a code review. This is a deliberate trade for flexible composition, not an accident. apps/cli/README.md:46-49

Asynchronous lifecycle is hard to debug

A row can be present and pending, loaded and failed, or active and waiting. A required failure is audited, but startup can also succeed with a warning that strands a consumer later. HMR applies deltas and can leave a mixed configuration after a failed replacement. The operator needs the audit output as well as the YAML.

The log grows and its format ages

Every model-visible fact needs an event and a projection. Compaction shrinks model context, not storage. Immutable generations make migration safe but accumulate files. A future version refuses to open; a downgrade does not guess at a newer vocabulary. The price of exact reconstruction is a compatibility obligation.

The loop is small, not simple

Turn, step, attempt, cancellation, pre-step, route binding, prompt admission, and tool recovery interlock. Treating the Agent interface as a thin facade understates the contract. Replacing the loop means preserving the observable session protocol rather than only returning model text.

Initiator scope is process-local

Attribution through AsyncLocalStorage helps in one process. A worker, an HTTP hop, a durable queue, or a restart must carry identity explicitly. A security decision based on ambient presence would be wrong. This is a boundary the architecture documents rather than hides.

None of these strains invalidates the design. They set the conditions under which it is a good fit.

The failing test, one more time

The request now looks different from chapter 1.

  • Composition decided that a loop, a session log, a tool registry, a model adapter, and a browser surface would exist before the prompt could move.
  • The turn engine accepted the prompt, claimed it from a durable inbox, and opened steps until the model stopped asking.
  • The log recorded every model-visible fact and made the request reconstructable.
  • Context assembly placed instructions in a system message, runtime facts in a late user snapshot, and tool declarations in the header.
  • The tool pipeline turned model calls into validated, policy-checked, ordered results.
  • Approval and sandboxing separated permission from capability.
  • Persistence made a crash recoverable and an interrupted tool call honestly unknown.
  • Delegation could move the log triage into a child with its own session and result path.
  • The browser rendered the same durable history through a separate plugin tree.

If the request were simpler, fewer boundaries would be justified. A single-turn read-only assistant needs no approval service, no sandbox, no fork, and possibly no durable log. If the request were more hostile, more boundaries would be needed: process isolation for tools, signed plugin packages, network policy, and a real security review. DSH sits between those extremes, built for a coding agent that can edit a checkout and run commands on a developer's machine.

What carries forward

The transferable core is small enough to state without the DSH vocabulary.

  1. Make the record primary. If the model saw it, make it reconstructable. Keep separate the facts, the projection the model reads, and the presentation a human sees.
  2. Keep one narrow execution spine. Let one component own the turn lifecycle, and attach everything else at explicit events or services. Do not let every capability become a second loop.
  3. Give every capability three roles. Define the interface, implement a provider, and write down the consumer. If you cannot name the consumer, you do not yet know the boundary.
  4. Make registration reversible and failures owned. A registration without a lifetime leaks; a failure without an owner either disappears or takes down too much.
  5. Decide before you act. Validation, approval, and confinement are separate questions. Keep the decision at the boundary and make refusal the default when the decision is unavailable.
  6. Be honest about durability. An accepted append, a durable write, and a rendered token are three different states. Name the barrier and test the crash on both sides of it.

The deep lesson from the source is not "use Cordis" or "use event sourcing." It is that a harness can be decomposed without hiding the hard parts. The event ordering is still explicit. The failure policy is still explicit. The security boundary is still named, along with what it does not cover. That is what makes the system understandable, and what makes it replaceable without becoming unpredictable.

The system can replace a part while it runs because ownership is explicit and the record does not belong to the part.
